title: 3.2.11 Bounded boundary data
text: Theorem 3.2.12 (Half-space Poisson integral) . 9ADD2DF19642 Let $f:\mathbb R^{d-1}\to \mathbb R$ be bounded and Lebesgue measurable, and let $c\in \mathbb R$. Then \[  u(x',t)=ct+\int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}P_ H((x',t),z)f(z)\, dz  \] is harmonic on $H$, and $|u(x',t)-ct|\leq \| f\| _\infty $. If $f$ is continuous at $z_0$, then $u(x',t)\to f(z_0)$ as $(x',t)\to (z_0,0)$ within $H$, with no restriction on the approach. Moreover $u(0,t)/t\to c$ as $t\to \infty $. Proof. We first verify the normalization AB2849CD8791 3.2.13 \begin{equation}  \int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}P_ H((x',t),z)\, dz=1. \end{equation} Translation and the substitution $z=x'+tw$ reduce the integral to $\frac{2}{s_{d-1}}\int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}(1+|w|^2)^{-d/2}\, dw$. The map \[  F(w)=\frac{(w,1)}{\sqrt{1+|w|^2}}  \] parametrizes the upper hemisphere. With $m=d-1$, its metric matrix is $DF^{\mathsf T}DF=(1+|w|^2)^{-1}I-(1+|w|^2)^{-2}ww^{\mathsf T}$. Its eigenvalues are $(1+|w|^2)^{-1}$ in the $m-1$ perpendicular directions and $(1+|w|^2)^{-2}$ in the direction of $w$. The square root of its determinant is $(1+|w|^2)^{-d/2}$. At $w=0$ this formula holds by continuity. The surface area formula and reflection in the equatorial plane show that the last integral is $s_{d-1}/2$, proving ( 3.2.13 ). This also treats $d=2$, when $m=1$ and there are no perpendicular directions. The weighted measure $|f(z)|\, dz$ satisfies ( 3.2.8 ), by the same integral at $(0,1)$. Applying the differentiation estimates in the proof of Theorem 3.2.6 to the positive and negative parts of $f$ proves harmonicity. The positivity and normalization of $P_ H$ give the stated bound. Fix $\varepsilon >0$. At a continuity point $z_0$, choose $\delta >0$ so that $|f(z)-f(z_0)|<\varepsilon $ for $|z-z_0|<\delta $. The contribution of this set to $|\int P_ H(x,z)(f(z)-f(z_0))\, dz|$ is at most $\varepsilon $. If $|x'-z_0|<\delta /2$ and $|z-z_0|\geq \delta $, then $|z-x'|\geq \delta /2$. Writing $s_{d-2}$ for the area of the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^{d-1}$ (in particular $s_0=2$), polar integration gives \[  \int _{|z-z_0|\geq \delta }P_ H(x,z)\, dz \leq \frac{2t}{s_{d-1}}s_{d-2}\int _{\delta /2}^{\infty }r^{-2}\, dr =\frac{4s_{d-2}}{s_{d-1}}\frac{t}{\delta }.  \] Thus \[  |u(x',t)-f(z_0)|\leq |c|t+\varepsilon + \frac{8s_{d-2}}{s_{d-1}}\| f\| _\infty \frac{t}{\delta }  \] near $(z_0,0)$. Letting $(x',t)\to (z_0,0)$ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves the boundary limit. Finally $|u(0,t)/t-c|\leq \| f\| _\infty /t\to 0$. $\square$ For continuous bounded boundary data, varying $c$ gives distinct harmonic solutions with the same finite boundary values. This states nonuniqueness without a growth condition; it does not classify all such solutions.

text: Theorem 3.3.9 . CAE5D89698DF Let $B=B(0,R)\subset \mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 2$, and let $\sigma $ be surface measure on $S=\partial B$. Let $\mu $ be a finite signed measure on $S$. For $\zeta \in S$ put $C_ s=\{ y\in S:|y-\zeta |\le s\} $. If $\mu (C_ s)/\sigma (C_ s)\to a\in \mathbb R$ as $s\downarrow 0$, then $P_ B\mu (t\zeta )\to a$ as $t\uparrow 1$. Proof. Subtract $a\sigma $, whose Poisson integral is the constant $a$. Thus $F(s)=\mu (C_ s)=o(A(s))$, where $A(s)=\sigma (C_ s)$. In particular $\mu (\{ \zeta \} )=0$. Fix $0<\delta <2R$ so that $|F(s)|\le \varepsilon A(s)$ for $0<s\le \delta $. The ball Poisson kernel at $t\zeta $ is a function of $s=|y-\zeta |$: \[  k_ t(s)=\frac{R^2(1-t^2)}{s_{d-1}R\, [R^2(1-t)^2+ts^2]^{d/2}}.  \] Here $s_{d-1}$ is the area of the unit sphere. This function is decreasing and smooth for $s\ge 0$, $0<t<1$. Integration of $k_ t(s)=k_ t(\delta )+\int _ s^\delta (-k_ t'(v))\, dv$ against the pushforward of $\mu |_{C_\delta }$, using finite signed Fubini, gives \[  \int _{C_\delta }k_ t(|y-\zeta |)\, d\mu =k_ t(\delta )F(\delta )+\int _0^\delta (-k_ t'(s))F(s)\, ds.  \] For each fixed $t$ all integrands are bounded and $\mu $ is finite, so this identity also holds when $F$ has jumps. Its absolute value is at most $\varepsilon \int _{C_\delta }k_ t\, d\sigma \le \varepsilon $, by positivity and normalization of the Poisson kernel. On $S\setminus C_\delta $, $\sup k_ t\to 0$, so the remaining integral tends to zero, bounded by $|\mu |(S)\sup _{s\ge \delta }k_ t(s)$. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. $\square$

Lemma 3.3.11 . 3FB36EAD186A Let $X$ be a compact metric space and $A\subset X$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a family of closed sets of positive diameter such that every $x\in A$ belongs to members of arbitrarily small diameter. There is a finite or countably infinite disjoint sequence $F_ j\in \mathcal F$ such that, in the finite case, $A\subset  igcup _ jF_ j$, and, in the infinite case, for every $j$, \[  A\subset  igcup _{i\le j}F_ i\  \cup  igcup _{i>j}N(F_ i,3\operatorname {diam}F_ i).  \] Here $N(F,r)=\{ x:d(x,F)<r\} $. If a finite complete measure $m$ satisfies $0<m(F)$ and $m(N(F,3\operatorname {diam}F))\le C m(F)$ for all eligible members, the sequence covers $A$ except for an $m$-null set. Proof. If $A=\varnothing $, choose the empty sequence. Otherwise choose any $F_1$. After $F_1,\ldots ,F_ j$, stop if they cover $A$. If they do not, a point outside their closed union belongs to sufficiently small members $F$ with $N(F,\operatorname {diam}F)$ disjoint from that union. Let $e_ j>0$ be the supremum of their diameters, and choose such an $F_{j+1}$ with diameter $>2e_ j/3$. All chosen sets are disjoint. Fix $x\in A\setminus  igcup _{i\le j}F_ i$ and choose a member $F$ containing $x$ whose diameter is so small that its diameter-neighborhood avoids the first $j$ sets. It must meet a later chosen $F_ k$ in that neighborhood. Otherwise it remains eligible forever, so all subsequent chosen diameters exceed $2\operatorname {diam}F/3$; choosing a point in each yields an infinite uniformly separated subset of compact $X$, impossible. At the first such $k$, $\operatorname {diam}F_ k>2\operatorname {diam}F/3$. Some point of $F_ k$ is within $\operatorname {diam}F$ of $F$, hence $d(x,F_ k)<2\operatorname {diam}F<3\operatorname {diam}F_ k$. This proves the covering assertion. In the measure case the outer measure of the uncovered set is at most $C\sum _{i>j}m(F_ i)$ for every $j$; the tail tends to zero because the sets are disjoint and $m(X)<\infty $. Completeness makes every subset of the resulting null set measurable. $\square$ Theorem 3.3.12 . 5F363A880A82 Let $S=\partial B(0,R)\subset \mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 2$, with completed surface measure $\sigma $. A finite signed measure $\mu =f\sigma +\mu _ s$ has, for $\sigma $-almost every $\zeta $, the derivative \[  \lim _{\substack {\zeta \in K\ \operatorname {diam}K	o 0}}  rac{\mu (K)}{\sigma (K)}=f(\zeta ).  \] The sets $K$ are closed spherical caps of positive diameter less than a hemisphere. title: Lemma 3.3.11
text: Lemma 3.3.11 . 3FB36EAD186A Let $X$ be a compact metric space and $A\subset X$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a family of closed sets of positive diameter such that every $x\in A$ belongs to members of arbitrarily small diameter. There is a finite or countably infinite disjoint sequence $F_ j\in \mathcal F$ such that, in the finite case, $A\subset \bigcup _ jF_ j$, and, in the infinite case, for every $j$, \[  A\subset \bigcup _{i\le j}F_ i\  \cup \bigcup _{i>j}N(F_ i,3\operatorname {diam}F_ i).  \] Here $N(F,r)=\{ x:d(x,F)<r\} $. If a finite complete measure $m$ satisfies $0<m(F)$ and $m(N(F,3\operatorname {diam}F))\le C m(F)$ for all eligible members, the sequence covers $A$ except for an $m$-null set. Proof. If $A=\varnothing $, choose the empty sequence. Otherwise choose any $F_1$. After $F_1,\ldots ,F_ j$, stop if they cover $A$. If they do not, a point outside their closed union belongs to sufficiently small members $F$ with $N(F,\operatorname {diam}F)$ disjoint from that union. Let $e_ j>0$ be the supremum of their diameters, and choose such an $F_{j+1}$ with diameter $>2e_ j/3$. All chosen sets are disjoint. Fix $x\in A\setminus \bigcup _{i\le j}F_ i$ and choose a member $F$ containing $x$ whose diameter is so small that its diameter-neighborhood avoids the first $j$ sets. It must meet a later chosen $F_ k$ in that neighborhood. Otherwise it remains eligible forever, so all subsequent chosen diameters exceed $2\operatorname {diam}F/3$; choosing a point in each yields an infinite uniformly separated subset of compact $X$, impossible. At the first such $k$, $\operatorname {diam}F_ k>2\operatorname {diam}F/3$. Some point of $F_ k$ is within $\operatorname {diam}F$ of $F$, hence $d(x,F_ k)<2\operatorname {diam}F<3\operatorname {diam}F_ k$. This proves the covering assertion. In the measure case the outer measure of the uncovered set is at most $C\sum _{i>j}m(F_ i)$ for every $j$; the tail tends to zero because the sets are disjoint and $m(X)<\infty $. Completeness makes every subset of the resulting null set measurable. $\square$

title: 3.3.15 Harmonic reflection across a sphere
text: Lemma 3.3.16 . B0CFE200676D A nonnegative harmonic function $h$ on a punctured neighborhood of $a$ has the form $c\Phi (\cdot -a)+v$, where $c\ge 0$, $v$ is harmonic across $a$, and $\Phi (z)=\log (1/|z|)$ for $d=2$, $\Phi (z)=|z|^{2-d}$ for $d\ge 3$. Proof. This is a short consequence of the checked local Riesz decomposition. On a sufficiently small ball define $u=h+\Phi (\cdot -a)$ off $a$ and $u(a)=+\infty $. The fundamental function tends to infinity, and $h\ge 0$; thus $u$ is lsc and is superharmonic, using locality off $a$ and the trivial supermean inequality at $a$. It is locally integrable by the checked local integrability theorem. Its positive Riesz measure $-\Delta u$ is supported at $a$, so it equals $b\delta _ a$ with $b\ge 0$. Since $-\Delta \Phi =c_ d\delta _ a$, where $c_2=2\pi $ and $c_ d=(d-2)s_{d-1}$ otherwise, Weyl's lemma gives $u=(b/c_ d)\Phi +v$ almost everywhere. Equality holds everywhere off $a$ by continuity. Hence $h=(b/c_ d-1)\Phi +v$ there, and its nonnegativity near $a$ forces $c=b/c_ d-1\ge 0$. This also proves removability when $h$ is bounded, or when a one-sided bounded harmonic function has a finite limit along one approach to $a$. $\square$ Theorem 3.3.17 . 14F410C2E770 Let $0<r<R$ and let $h$ be continuous on the closed annulus $r\le |x-a|\le R$, harmonic on its interior, and zero on $|x-a|=R$. It has a harmonic extension across that sphere to $r<|x-a|<R+\varepsilon $ for some $\varepsilon >0$. Proof. First, odd reflection across a hyperplane preserves harmonicity for a harmonic function continuous and zero at that plane. The reflected function is continuous; at a center on the plane its spherical means vanish by the reflection symmetry, and away from the plane sufficiently small spheres have the usual harmonic mean property. The checked local mean characterization therefore proves harmonicity across the plane. Translate $a=0$. Add a sufficiently large positive multiple of $\log (R/|x|)$ if $d=2$, or of $|x|^{2-d}-R^{2-d}$ otherwise, so that the result is nonnegative on the inner sphere. The minimum principle makes it nonnegative throughout the annulus. These added functions already extend harmonically across the outer sphere, so it suffices to treat $h\ge 0$. Choose $b$ on the outer sphere and invert about a sphere centered at $b$. The outer sphere minus $b$ becomes a hyperplane, and the inner closed ball becomes a compact ball strictly in one of its half-spaces. The Kelvin transform is harmonic outside that compact ball in the half-space, continuous and zero at its planar boundary. Reflect it oddly. Applying the inverse Kelvin transform gives a harmonic extension on a neighborhood of the original closed annulus, except possibly at $b$. On its exterior side this extension is nonpositive, since the reflected function is nonpositive and the Kelvin multiplier is positive. On the interior side it tends to zero at $b$, so it is bounded above on a punctured neighborhood of $b$. Apply the preceding lemma to a constant minus this extension. Its singular coefficient must vanish because the extension has limit zero along the interior approach. Thus the singularity at $b$ is removable. Compactness of the outer sphere gives one $\varepsilon >0$ valid around the whole sphere. Finally subtract the added radial harmonic function. $\square$

title: 3.5.1 Harmonic lowering and greatest harmonic minorants
search_title: Harmonic lowering and greatest harmonic minorants
text: The following arguments use superharmonic functions in the nontrivial componentwise sense. Harmonic lowering $L_ Bu$ equals the Poisson integral of $u|_{\partial B}$ in $B\Subset \Omega $, and equals $u$ outside $B$. The checked comparison and Poisson boundary lower-limit statements show that $L_ Bu$ is superharmonic and $L_ Bu\le u$: at a boundary point it is lsc, and its sphere averages are at most those of $u$, with the same center value. In $B$ it is harmonic, and elsewhere locality applies. Lemma 3.5.2 . AC0C4669DCBF Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty family of superharmonic functions on an open set $\Omega $, closed under pairwise minimum and under every harmonic lowering. Its infimum is harmonic or identically $-\infty $ on each component. Proof. On a ball $B\Subset \Omega $ its infimum is also $\inf _{u\in \mathcal F}L_ Bu$, since $L_ Bu\le u$ and $L_ Bu\in \mathcal F$. The lowered harmonic functions form a downward directed family: $L_ B(\min (u,v))\le \min (L_ Bu,L_ Bv)$ by positivity of the Poisson kernel. A downward directed family of harmonic functions has harmonic infimum or infimum identically $-\infty $ on a ball. To see this from the checked Harnack convergence theorem, negate and restrict to the cofinal subfamily above one fixed member; its differences from that member are nonnegative harmonic. If bounded at one point, Harnack chains bound them on compact subsets, and harmonic compactness shows their directed supremum harmonic. If unbounded at a point, Harnack chains make the supremum infinity everywhere. Thus the infimum is locally harmonic or locally identically $-\infty $. The regions of these two alternatives are disjoint open sets; connectedness of each component leaves only one alternative. $\square$ Theorem 3.5.3 . 2791D284428C Let $u$ be superharmonic on $\Omega $ and $W\subset \Omega $ open. Choose balls $B_ j\Subset W$ covering $W$, with each chosen ball repeated infinitely often, and set $u_0=u$, $u_ j=L_{B_ j}u_{j-1}$. Then $u_ j$ decreases to $u_\infty $, equal to $u$ outside $W$, and harmonic or identically $-\infty $ on each component of $W$. If $u$ has a harmonic minorant on $W$, the restriction $u_\infty |_ W$ is its unique greatest harmonic minorant, independent of the ball sequence. This operation is additive on superharmonic functions having harmonic minorants. Proof. Lowering makes the sequence decrease and leaves it fixed outside $W$. On each fixed ball, the subsequence of stages just lowered there is harmonic and decreases to the same limit; the checked harmonic monotone convergence theorem makes that limit harmonic or $-\infty $. Connectedness propagates the alternative as in the preceding proof. If $v$ is any harmonic minorant on $W$, positivity of the Poisson kernel proves inductively $v\le u_ j$ there. Thus $v\le u_\infty \le u$, which excludes $-\infty $ and proves maximality and uniqueness. For two functions use the same sequence of balls. Linearity of each lowering gives $(u+v)_ j=u_ j+v_ j$; the limits are finite on $W$ when harmonic minorants exist, so their sum is the corresponding greatest harmonic minorant. No claim is made that the unregularized $u_\infty $ is superharmonic across $\partial W$. $\square$

title: 3.5.4 Minimal Green functions on general open sets
search_title: Minimal Green functions on general open sets
text: Write $\Phi _ a(x)=\Phi (x-a)$, with the normalization of Lemma 3.3.16 . A minimal Green function on an open set $\Omega $ is a nonnegative kernel $G$ such that $G(a,\cdot )=\Phi _ a+h_ a$, $h_ a$ harmonic on $\Omega $, and $G(a,\cdot )\le \Phi _ a+w$ whenever $w$ is superharmonic on $\Omega $ and $\Phi _ a+w\ge 0$. At $a$, both kernels have value infinity; differences of singular kernels below mean the harmonic extension of their difference off the pole. Theorem 3.5.5 . F3C6870EA9A8 For $a\in \Omega $ put $\mathcal B_ a=\{ \Phi _ a+w\ge 0:w\text{ superharmonic on }\Omega \} $. A minimal Green function exists exactly when all these classes are nonempty, and then $G(a,\cdot )=\inf \mathcal B_ a$ and it is unique. Existence holds for every open set if $d\ge 3$, every bounded open set if $d=2$, every open subset of a Greenian open set, and every planar open set which is not dense or is disconnected. The whole plane, and the plane minus a closed discrete set, have no Green function. In $\mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 3$, the Green function is $\Phi _ a$. Proof. The class $\mathcal B_ a$ is closed under minimum and lowering on balls away from $a$, since $\Phi _ a$ is harmonic there and lowering preserves superharmonicity of $w$. Its infimum $v$ is nonnegative and harmonic away from $a$ by Lemma 3.5.2 . On a ball about $a$, every member dominates the ball Green function: their harmonic singularities cancel and the superharmonic difference has nonnegative boundary lower limits. Hence $v$ also dominates that ball Green function. The local Bôcher lemma gives $v=c\Phi _ a+h$ with $c\ge 0$; the preceding domination forces $c\ge 1$. This expression defines harmonic $h$ across $a$ and on all of $\Omega $. Now $v/c=\Phi _ a+h/c\ge 0$ belongs to $\mathcal B_ a$, so $v\le v/c\le v$. If $c>1$, this would force $v=0$ off $a$, contradicting the ball domination. Thus $c=1$, and $v$ is the required minimal kernel. Uniqueness and necessity follow at once from the definition. For $d\ge 3$, $\Phi _ a\ge 0$ is an admissible member. For a bounded planar set, $\Phi _ a+C\ge 0$ for a sufficiently large constant. Restriction of an existing Green kernel supplies a member on any smaller open set. If a planar open set avoids a closed ball, translate and dilate so that it avoids $\overline{B(0,1)}$. For $a,y$ in it, \[  \log \frac{2|a||y|}{|a-y|} =\Phi _ a(y)+\log |y|+\log (2|a|)\ge 0,  \] since $|1/a-1/y|<2$. The last two terms are harmonic in $y$ there. For a disconnected planar open set, each component avoids a ball in another component and is Greenian. For a pole in one component, extend its harmonic correction by $-\Phi _ a$ on all the others; the resulting admissible member is zero on those other components. This proves existence for the union. A planar Green kernel would have a harmonic correction $h_ a\ge -\Phi _ a=\log |\cdot -a|$, which tends to infinity at infinity. On arbitrarily large circles the minimum principle would then force $h_ a(0)$ to exceed every constant, impossible. A minimal kernel is bounded outside every ball $B\Subset \Omega $ containing its pole. Indeed let $m=\max _{\partial B}G(a,\cdot )>0$, and replace it outside $B$ by $\min (G(a,\cdot ),2m)$. This agrees with $G$ near the sphere, is superharmonic, and after subtracting $\Phi _ a$ is superharmonic across the pole. Minimality bounds $G$ by this replacement. They are symmetric, zero between different components, and strictly positive within one component. They are jointly continuous off the diagonal and tend to infinity jointly at the diagonal. Restriction is admissible, proving domain monotonicity. Along an exhaustion the increasing limit is bounded above by $G_\Omega $ off the pole, hence harmonic there. The limit is a nonnegative admissible kernel and is therefore $G_\Omega $ by minimality. Every harmonic minorant $v$ of $G(a,\cdot )$ satisfies $v\le 0$, since $G-v$ is admissible and minimality gives $G\le G-v$. Thus its greatest harmonic minorant is zero. In the simultaneous lowering process of the preceding theorem, applied to $G(a,\cdot )=\Phi _ a+h_ a$, the harmonic correction is invariant, so \[  0=(\Phi _ a)_\infty +h_ a,\qquad G(a,y)=\Phi _ a(y)-(\Phi _ a)_\infty (y).  \] We verify that $q(a,y)=(\Phi _ a)_\infty (y)$ is harmonic in $a$ for each fixed $y$. Such a cover is obtained by covering the compact layers of a nested compact exhaustion by finitely many small balls lying in adjacent exhaustion layers; only finitely many distinct balls meet each compact subset. Its union of boundary spheres $C$ is relatively closed. At a finite lowering stage, integration of $\Phi _ a(z)$ against the successive compact-sphere Poisson kernels is harmonic in $a$ away from those spheres and, until a ball containing $y$ has been used, possibly away from $y$. Differentiation is justified locally by positive distance from the finite union of spheres and bounded derivatives of the fundamental kernel; iterated finite integrals preserve those bounds. title: Theorem 3.5.5
text: Theorem 3.5.5 . F3C6870EA9A8 For $a\in \Omega $ put $\mathcal B_ a=\{ \Phi _ a+w\ge 0:w\text{ superharmonic on }\Omega \} $. A minimal Green function exists exactly when all these classes are nonempty, and then $G(a,\cdot )=\inf \mathcal B_ a$ and it is unique. Existence holds for every open set if $d\ge 3$, every bounded open set if $d=2$, every open subset of a Greenian open set, and every planar open set which is not dense or is disconnected. The whole plane, and the plane minus a closed discrete set, have no Green function. In $\mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 3$, the Green function is $\Phi _ a$. Proof. The class $\mathcal B_ a$ is closed under minimum and lowering on balls away from $a$, since $\Phi _ a$ is harmonic there and lowering preserves superharmonicity of $w$. Its infimum $v$ is nonnegative and harmonic away from $a$ by Lemma 3.5.2 . On a ball about $a$, every member dominates the ball Green function: their harmonic singularities cancel and the superharmonic difference has nonnegative boundary lower limits. Hence $v$ also dominates that ball Green function. The local Bôcher lemma gives $v=c\Phi _ a+h$ with $c\ge 0$; the preceding domination forces $c\ge 1$. This expression defines harmonic $h$ across $a$ and on all of $\Omega $. Now $v/c=\Phi _ a+h/c\ge 0$ belongs to $\mathcal B_ a$, so $v\le v/c\le v$. If $c>1$, this would force $v=0$ off $a$, contradicting the ball domination. Thus $c=1$, and $v$ is the required minimal kernel. Uniqueness and necessity follow at once from the definition. For $d\ge 3$, $\Phi _ a\ge 0$ is an admissible member. For a bounded planar set, $\Phi _ a+C\ge 0$ for a sufficiently large constant. Restriction of an existing Green kernel supplies a member on any smaller open set. If a planar open set avoids a closed ball, translate and dilate so that it avoids $\overline{B(0,1)}$. For a disconnected planar open set, each component avoids a ball in another component and is Greenian. For a pole in one component, extend its harmonic correction by $-\Phi _ a$ on all the others; the resulting admissible member is zero on those other components. This proves existence for the union. A planar Green kernel would have a harmonic correction $h_ a\ge -\Phi _ a=\log |\cdot -a|$, which tends to infinity at infinity. On arbitrarily large circles the minimum principle would then force $h_ a(0)$ to exceed every constant, impossible. This agrees with $G$ near the sphere, is superharmonic, and after subtracting $\Phi _ a$ is superharmonic across the pole. Minimality bounds $G$ by this replacement. On a plane minus a closed discrete set, this bound and the Bôcher lemma remove every deleted point as a bounded harmonic singularity. The resulting nonnegative kernel has a harmonic correction on the whole plane, contradicting the preceding minimum-principle argument. Its constant must be zero because $G\ge 0$ and $\Phi _ a\to 0$ at infinity. $\square$

title: 3.5.7 Potentials and global Riesz decomposition
text:
Throughout this section $G_\Omega $ is the unnormalized minimal Green kernel, $-\Delta G_\Omega (\cdot ,y)=c_ d\delta _ y$. Measures are positive Radon measures; they need not have finite total mass. A potential means $p=G_\Omega \mu $ which is not identically infinity on any component. Theorem 3.5.8 . 977ECF0867E0 The integral $G_\Omega \mu $ is lsc and supermean, hence superharmonic on every component where it is nontrivial. Every finite measure has a potential. For any potential, \[  -\Delta (G_\Omega \mu )=c_ d\mu  \] in distributions. Its greatest harmonic minorant is zero. It is harmonic on an open set exactly when that set has $\mu $-measure zero. Two potentials whose difference is harmonic almost everywhere on an open set have equal measures there. If $S\subset \Omega $ is open, $\mu $ is supported in $S$ and $G_\Omega \mu $ is a potential, then $G_\Omega \mu =G_ S\mu +h$ on $S$ with $h\ge 0$ harmonic. Reciprocity $\int G\mu \, d
u =\int G
u \, d\mu $ holds in $[0,\infty ]$. Proof. Fatou's lemma applied to the nonnegative continuous extended kernel gives lsc; Tonelli and the supermean inequality for each pole give supermeans. If $\mu $ is finite and gives zero mass to a closed interior ball containing $x$, the bound for $G(x,\cdot )$ outside that ball makes its potential finite at $x$, hence superharmonic on that component. Split a finite measure into its part on a small interior ball and its complement. Each part misses some interior ball in the component, so both have superharmonic potentials and their sum is superharmonic. Apply this separately to every component, using that $G$ vanishes between components. A potential $p$ is locally integrable by superharmonic local integrability. For $\varphi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$, \[  \iint G(x,y)|\Delta \varphi (x)|\, dx\, d\mu (y) =\int p(x)|\Delta \varphi (x)|\, dx<\infty .  \] Thus signed Fubini is legitimate, and the fundamental-solution identity plus harmonicity of the correction gives $\int p\Delta \varphi =-c_ d\int \varphi \, d\mu $. In particular a harmonic potential has zero measure; more generally subtracting the distributional identities proves equality of measures wherever the difference is harmonic. If $\mu (U)=0$, Weyl's lemma gives a harmonic representative on $U$; canonical representative uniqueness identifies it pointwise with $p$. For the greatest minorant use the same sequence of harmonic lowerings for $p$ and for every kernel $G(\cdot ,y)$. Induction and nonnegative Tonelli show $p_ j(x)=\int G_ j(x,y)\, d\mu (y)$. For each $y$, $G_ j(x,y)\downarrow 0$, because the greatest harmonic minorant of the minimal Green kernel is zero. In each connected component choose $x_0$ with $p(x_0)<\infty $. Dominated convergence gives $p_\infty (x_0)=0$; its nonnegative harmonic minorant is therefore zero on that component by the minimum principle. This is a componentwise argument, even when $\Omega $ is disconnected. On $S$, domain monotonicity gives $0\le G_ S\mu \le p$. Both potentials are locally integrable; their distributional difference is harmonic and nonnegative almost everywhere, hence a nonnegative harmonic $h$. Equality $p=G_ S\mu +h$ holds everywhere by uniqueness of superharmonic representatives. Finally symmetry of $G$ and nonnegative Tonelli give reciprocity, including infinite values. None of these arguments separates divergent fundamental and harmonic-correction integrals. $\square$ Theorem 3.5.9 . 9453A8C660CC Let $u$ be superharmonic on a Greenian open set $\Omega $. Its unique Riesz measure is $
u =-\Delta u/c_ d$. For each open $W\Subset \Omega $, \[  u=G_ W(
u |_ W)+h_ W\quad \hbox{on }W,  \] where $h_ W$ is the greatest harmonic minorant there. If $u\ge 0$ on $\Omega $, the same formula holds globally with $W=\Omega $ and a nonnegative harmonic $h$. Thus a nonnegative superharmonic function is a Green potential exactly when its greatest harmonic minorant is zero. Proof. The checked distributional characterization gives the positive Radon measure $
u $. We first suppose $u$ is bounded below by a constant $m$ on its Greenian domain $D$ (either $D=W\Subset \Omega $, or $D=\Omega $ and $m=0$). For a compact $K\subset D$ put $p_ K=G_ D(
u |_ K)$, a potential of a finite measure. The locally integrable difference $u-p_ K$ has nonpositive Laplacian, so it has a superharmonic representative $w_ K$, and $u=w_ K+p_ K$ everywhere by canonical representative uniqueness. The function $p_ K$ is bounded outside some compact neighborhood $K'\Subset D$. Here is the required uniformity: cover $K$ by finitely many small balls whose closures lie in $D$. On each, Harnack chains bound $G_ D(x,y)$ for $y$ in its smaller concentric ball by a fixed multiple of $G_ D(x,y_ i)$, whenever $x$ lies outside the union of the larger balls. Each fixed-pole kernel is bounded away from its pole; integrating the resulting finite uniform bound against $
u |_ K$ proves the assertion. Choose $K'$ containing these larger closed balls. On $D\setminus K'$, $w_ K=u-p_ K\ge m-M$; on $K'$ it is bounded below by lsc and compactness. Hence $w_ K$ has a constant harmonic minorant on all of $D$. The greatest-minorant operation is additive, and $p_ K$ has greatest minorant zero. Thus $H_ Du=H_ Dw_ K\ge m$ because $u\ge m$. Consequently $w_ K\ge m$ and $p_ K\le u-m$. Exhaust $D$ by increasing compact $K_ j$. Monotone convergence gives $p=G_ D(
u |_ D)\le u-m$. This is finite almost everywhere, hence a potential. Its Riesz measure is $
u |_ D$, so $u-p$ is harmonic in distributions and has a harmonic representative $h$. Canonical uniqueness gives $u=p+h$ everywhere, and additivity of greatest minorants makes $h=H_ Du$. When $m=0$, $h\ge 0$. Applying this construction to every relatively compact $W$ proves the local assertion without assuming $u$ bounded below on the entire $\Omega $. Uniqueness of $
u $ follows from its distributional identity, and the last characterization follows from the zero-minorant property of potentials. $\square$

title: 3.5.10 Continuity of potentials and bounded densities
search_title: Continuity of potentials and bounded densities
text: Theorem 3.5.11 . 64E880580F0E Let $\mu $ have compact support $K\Subset \Omega $. If $(G_\Omega \mu )|_ K$ is continuous at $a\in K$, then $G_\Omega \mu $ is continuous at $a$, in the extended sense. If $G_\Omega \mu $ is finite on $K$, then for every $\varepsilon >0$ there is a compact $C\subset K$ with $\mu (K\setminus C)<\varepsilon $ for which $G_\Omega (\mu |_ C)$ is finite and continuous throughout $\Omega $. Proof. Near $K$ the Green potential differs from its fundamental potential by a harmonic function. Both potentials are locally integrable and have the same distributional Laplacian, so Weyl's lemma gives a harmonic difference. Adding that harmonic function preserves superharmonicity; canonical representatives then identify the equality everywhere, including infinite values. No joint continuity of a cancelled diagonal kernel is assumed. It suffices to prove the first assertion for $U\mu (x)=\int \Phi (x-y)d\mu (y)$. If $U\mu (a)=\infty $, lsc suffices. Otherwise choose a small ball $B$ about $a$ and split $\mu =\mu '+\mu ''$, with $\mu '=\mu |_ B$, so that the local singular integral $U\mu '(a)<\eta $. In the planar case take all relevant distances less than one so this local kernel is nonnegative. The remainder $U\mu ''$ is harmonic near $a$. If $z_ x\in K$ is a nearest point to $x$, then $z_ x\to a$ as $x\to a$, and $|z_ x-y|\le 2|x-y|$ for $y\in K$. For $d\ge 3$ this gives $U\mu '(x)\le 2^{d-2}U\mu '(z_ x)$. For $d=2$ it gives $U\mu '(x)\le U\mu '(z_ x)+(\log 2)\mu '(B)$. The restriction of $U\mu '$ to $K$ is continuous at $a$, being the difference of the assumed continuous restriction of $U\mu $ and the harmonic remainder. Thus the limsup of the local contribution is at most $2^{d-2}\eta $, or $\eta +(\log 2)\mu (B)$ in dimension two. In that case $\mu (\{ a\} )=0$ by finiteness of the potential, so $\mu (B)\to 0$ as the radius shrinks. The harmonic remainder is continuous; letting $\eta \to 0$ proves continuity. For the second assertion, Lusin's theorem gives compact $C\subset K$ with lost mass less than $\varepsilon $ and $G\mu |_ C$ finite continuous. On $C$, $G(\mu |_ C)=G\mu -G(\mu |_{K\setminus C})$ is upper semicontinuous, since the second term is lsc; it is also lsc. It is therefore continuous on $C$, and the first assertion gives continuity at every point of $C$. Off $C$ it is harmonic. This proves global finite continuity. $\square$ Theorem 3.5.12 . 9CF388990FE4 If $f\in L^1(\Omega )\cap L^\infty (\Omega )$, then $G_\Omega f$ is finite continuous on $\Omega $. For a ball and compactly supported measure its potential tends to zero at every boundary point. More generally suppose $\Omega $ is connected, has finite volume for $d\ge 3$, and is bounded for $d=2$. If $G_\Omega (x,y_0)\to 0$ as $x\to a\in \partial \Omega $ for one $y_0\in \Omega $, then $G_\Omega f(x)\to 0$ for every bounded measurable $f$. Proof. Separate the positive and negative parts of $f$. They are finite measures, so have superharmonic potentials. On an interior ball, the contribution from its complement is harmonic; the local contribution differs from a fundamental potential by a harmonic function. Its singular integral over a ball of radius $r$ is uniformly at most $\| f\| _\infty s_{d-1}r^2/2$ for $d\ge 3$, and $2\pi \| f\| _\infty \int _0^ r s\log (1/s)ds$ in the plane, after adding a harmless local constant. These bounds tend to zero. To justify that a ball centered elsewhere has no larger integral of the radial decreasing positive kernel, use its layer-cake representation: intersection with every centered superlevel ball has volume at most the smaller of the two ball volumes. The nonsingular part is continuous by dominated convergence, proving the first assertion and finiteness. For the boundary assertions, Harnack chains in the pole variable make $G(x,\cdot )\to 0$ uniformly on any fixed compact subset when it tends to zero at one pole. The explicit ball kernel supplies this condition at every ball boundary point, so compactly supported potentials tend to zero. Exhaust $\Omega $ by compact $K_ j$. In dimension at least three, $G(x,y)\le |x-y|^{2-d}$, and the layer-cake estimate just proved yields \[  \sup _ x\int _{\Omega \setminus K_ j}G(x,y)|f(y)|dy \le \tfrac 12s_{d-1}\| f\| _\infty (|\Omega \setminus K_ j|/v_ d)^{2/d}\longrightarrow 0.  \] For a bounded planar domain choose $D>\operatorname {diam}\Omega $; $G(x,y)\le \log (D/|x-y|)$ by minimality, and the same estimate is the integral of this radial kernel over a disk of the tail's area, tending to zero. Thus the compact-support integrals approximate $Gf$ uniformly in $x$, and their boundary limits are zero. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.5.11
text: Theorem 3.5.11 . 64E880580F0E Let $\mu $ have compact support $K\Subset \Omega $. If $(G_\Omega \mu )|_ K$ is continuous at $a\in K$, then $G_\Omega \mu $ is continuous at $a$, in the extended sense. If $G_\Omega \mu $ is finite on $K$, then for every $\varepsilon >0$ there is a compact $C\subset K$ with $\mu (K\setminus C)<\varepsilon $ for which $G_\Omega (\mu |_ C)$ is finite and continuous throughout $\Omega $. Proof. Near $K$ the Green potential differs from its fundamental potential by a harmonic function. Both potentials are locally integrable and have the same distributional Laplacian, so Weyl's lemma gives a harmonic difference. Adding that harmonic function preserves superharmonicity; canonical representatives then identify the equality everywhere, including infinite values. No joint continuity of a cancelled diagonal kernel is assumed. It suffices to prove the first assertion for $U\mu (x)=\int \Phi (x-y)d\mu (y)$. If $U\mu (a)=\infty $, lsc suffices. Otherwise choose a small ball $B$ about $a$ and split $\mu =\mu '+\mu ''$, with $\mu '=\mu |_ B$, so that the local singular integral $U\mu '(a)<\eta $. In the planar case take all relevant distances less than one so this local kernel is nonnegative. The remainder $U\mu ''$ is harmonic near $a$. If $z_ x\in K$ is a nearest point to $x$, then $z_ x\to a$ as $x\to a$, and $|z_ x-y|\le 2|x-y|$ for $y\in K$. For $d\ge 3$ this gives $U\mu '(x)\le 2^{d-2}U\mu '(z_ x)$. For $d=2$ it gives $U\mu '(x)\le U\mu '(z_ x)+(\log 2)\mu '(B)$. The restriction of $U\mu '$ to $K$ is continuous at $a$, being the difference of the assumed continuous restriction of $U\mu $ and the harmonic remainder. Thus the limsup of the local contribution is at most $2^{d-2}\eta $, or $\eta +(\log 2)\mu (B)$ in dimension two. In that case $\mu (\{ a\} )=0$ by finiteness of the potential, so $\mu (B)\to 0$ as the radius shrinks. The harmonic remainder is continuous; letting $\eta \to 0$ proves continuity. For the second assertion, Lusin's theorem gives compact $C\subset K$ with lost mass less than $\varepsilon $ and $G\mu |_ C$ finite continuous. On $C$, $G(\mu |_ C)=G\mu -G(\mu |_{K\setminus C})$ is upper semicontinuous, since the second term is lsc; it is also lsc. It is therefore continuous on $C$, and the first assertion gives continuity at every point of $C$. Off $C$ it is harmonic. This proves global finite continuity. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.5.12
text: Theorem 3.5.12 . 9CF388990FE4 If $f\in L^1(\Omega )\cap L^\infty (\Omega )$, then $G_\Omega f$ is finite continuous on $\Omega $. For a ball and compactly supported measure its potential tends to zero at every boundary point. More generally suppose $\Omega $ is connected, has finite volume for $d\ge 3$, and is bounded for $d=2$. If $G_\Omega (x,y_0)\to 0$ as $x\to a\in \partial \Omega $ for one $y_0\in \Omega $, then $G_\Omega f(x)\to 0$ for every bounded measurable $f$. Proof. Separate the positive and negative parts of $f$. They are finite measures, so have superharmonic potentials. On an interior ball, the contribution from its complement is harmonic; the local contribution differs from a fundamental potential by a harmonic function. Its singular integral over a ball of radius $r$ is uniformly at most $\| f\| _\infty s_{d-1}r^2/2$ for $d\ge 3$, and $2\pi \| f\| _\infty \int _0^ r s\log (1/s)ds$ in the plane, after adding a harmless local constant. These bounds tend to zero. To justify that a ball centered elsewhere has no larger integral of the radial decreasing positive kernel, use its layer-cake representation: intersection with every centered superlevel ball has volume at most the smaller of the two ball volumes. The nonsingular part is continuous by dominated convergence, proving the first assertion and finiteness. For the boundary assertions, Harnack chains in the pole variable make $G(x,\cdot )\to 0$ uniformly on any fixed compact subset when it tends to zero at one pole. The explicit ball kernel supplies this condition at every ball boundary point, so compactly supported potentials tend to zero. Exhaust $\Omega $ by compact $K_ j$. In dimension at least three, $G(x,y)\le |x-y|^{2-d}$, and the layer-cake estimate just proved yields \[  \sup _ x\int _{\Omega \setminus K_ j}G(x,y)|f(y)|dy \le \tfrac 12s_{d-1}\| f\| _\infty (|\Omega \setminus K_ j|/v_ d)^{2/d}\longrightarrow 0.  \] For a bounded planar domain choose $D>\operatorname {diam}\Omega $; $G(x,y)\le \log (D/|x-y|)$ by minimality, and the same estimate is the integral of this radial kernel over a disk of the tail's area, tending to zero. Thus the compact-support integrals approximate $Gf$ uniformly in $x$, and their boundary limits are zero. $\square$

title: 3.5.13 The generalized Laplacian
text: For a continuous function $u$, write $\widetilde\Delta u(x)=\lim _{r\downarrow 0}2d(M_ ru(x)-u(x))/r^2$ whenever this finite limit exists, where $M_ r$ is the normalized sphere mean. Theorem 3.5.14 . 27ABF8BDD497 For bounded continuous $f\in L^1(\Omega )$ on a Greenian open set, $\widetilde\Delta (G_\Omega f)=-c_ df$ pointwise. If $u$ is continuous and $\widetilde\Delta u=0$ on an open set, then $u$ is harmonic there. Proof. Near a fixed $x$, the contribution of the measure outside a small closed ball is harmonic, and the local Green potential differs from its fundamental potential by a harmonic function. Harmonic functions contribute zero to the generalized Laplacian. The sphere average of $\Phi (\cdot -y)$ at center $x$ is $\Phi (r)$ when $|x-y|\le r$ and $\Phi (x-y)$ otherwise. For the second case this is the harmonic mean property. For the first, rotation invariance gives a radial harmonic function of $y$ inside the sphere, smooth there by differentiation, hence constant, with its value at the center equal to $\Phi (r)$. Here is uniform control at the sphere: its surface measure in any ball of radius $s$ centered on or near it is at most $Cs^{d-1}$, by finitely many bounded graph charts. Layer-cake integration therefore bounds its fundamental singular integral on such a cap by $Cs$ for $d\ge 3$, and by $Cs(1+|\log s|)$ for $d=2$. These bounds tend to zero uniformly in the pole. The remaining kernel is uniformly continuous, proving continuity across the sphere. Consequently \[  \frac{2d}{r^2}(M_ rGf(x)-Gf(x)) =\frac{2d}{r^2}\int _{|y-x|<r}[\Phi (r)-\Phi (x-y)]f(y)dy.  \] The bracket is nonpositive. Its absolute integral is $\pi r^2/2$ for $d=2$, since $2\pi \int _0^ r s\log (r/s)ds=\pi r^2/2$; for $d\ge 3$ it is $s_{d-1}r^2(1/2-1/d)$. Thus the expression for constant $f(x)$ is exactly $-c_ df(x)$, while the error is at most $c_ d\sup _{|y-x|<r}|f(y)-f(x)|$, tending to zero. For the converse fix a ball $B\Subset \Omega $, let $H$ be the continuous Poisson solution with boundary values $u$, and let $w=G_ B1$, continuous, zero at the boundary, with $\widetilde\Delta w=-c_ d$ by the first part. For $t>0$, both $u-H+tw$ and $H-u+tw$ have strictly negative generalized Laplacian. Hence at every point they satisfy the strict local supermean inequality for all sufficiently small radii. The elementary minimum principle for continuous locally supermean functions, proved by the open-and-closed minimum set argument, implies they are nonnegative on $B$ because their boundary values are zero. Let $t\downarrow 0$; then $u=H$. As $B$ was arbitrary, $u$ is harmonic. $\square$

title: 4.3.1 Global polar functions and exact compact pole sets
search_title: Global polar functions and exact compact pole sets
text: Theorem 4.3.2 . 253540032CE5 Every polar subset $A\subset \mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 2$, is contained in the infinite locus of an entire superharmonic function. If $a\notin A$, that function can be chosen finite at $a$. For $d\ge 3$ it can be chosen as a Newtonian potential of a finite positive measure. If $K\Subset \Omega $ is compact and polar in a Greenian open set, there is a finite compactly supported measure $\mu $ on $\Omega $ with $G_\Omega \mu =\infty $ on $K$ and $G_\Omega \mu <\infty $ everywhere else in $\Omega $. Proof. We use the checked Foundations polar globalization : every bounded polar set has a finite compactly supported fundamental measure whose potential is infinite on that set. For the prescribed point put $A_ j=A\cap \{ 1/j\le |x-a|\le j\} $. Apply that result and restrict the resulting measure to $\{ |y-a|>1/(2j)\} $. The removed part has a bounded kernel at each point of $A_ j$, so the restricted fundamental potential $p_ j$ is still infinite on $A_ j$ and finite at $a$. In dimension at least three choose $b_ j>0$ so that $\sum b_ j(\mu _ j(\mathbb R^ d)+p_ j(a))<\infty $. Then $\mu =\sum b_ j\mu _ j$ is finite and its positive Newtonian potential is finite at $a$ and infinite on $A=\bigcup A_ j$, by Tonelli. In dimension two set $q_ j=p_ j-m_ j$, where $m_ j$ is the finite infimum of $p_ j$ on $\overline{B(a,j)}$. Such an infimum is finite by lsc and local integrability. Choose $b_ j>0$ with $\sum b_ jq_ j(a)<\infty $. For each fixed integer $k$, the tail $\sum _{j\ge k}b_ jq_ j$ is a monotone sum of nonnegative superharmonic functions on $B(a,k)$, finite at $a$; it is superharmonic there. Adding the finite initial sum gives an entire superharmonic function, finite at $a$ and infinite on $A$. Without a prescribed point, first choose $a$ outside the polar (hence null) set. For the last assertion first treat $K$ contained in an interior ball $B$. Its normalized ball capacity is zero by the checked polar zero capacity . Choose decreasing compact neighborhoods $K_ j\Subset B$ with intersection $K$; their capacitary potentials $v_ j$ lie in $[0,1]$, equal one near $K$, and decrease to zero off $K$. Indeed the limit is bounded harmonic off $K$, extends harmonically across $K$ by polar removability, and is dominated by the zero-minorant potential $v_1$, so is zero. On every compact subset of $B\setminus K$ this convergence is uniform by Dini. Pass to a subsequence such that both $\operatorname {cap}_ B(K_ j)<2^{-j}$ and $v_ j<2^{-j}$ on the first $j$ members of a compact exhaustion of $B\setminus K$ (and put every support in one fixed compact subset of $B$). This is possible by decreasing capacity continuity and the preceding uniform convergence. Write $v_ j=G_ B\mu _ j$, scaling the normalized Riesz measures by $1/c_ d$ for our kernel. Then $\sum \mu _ j(B)<\infty $. The potential of $\mu =\sum \mu _ j$ is $\sum v_ j$, infinite on $K$ and finite off $K$ in $B$. Its fundamental potential differs by a harmonic function on $B$; thus it has exactly the same finiteness set there. Off the common compact support it is finite automatically. The same distributional/harmonic-correction argument transfers it to $G_\Omega \mu $ without changing its poles. For general compact $K\Subset \Omega $, choose finitely many closed balls inside slightly larger interior balls whose interiors cover $K$; apply the construction to the polar compact intersections with these closed balls and add their measures. The sum is finite, compactly supported in $\Omega $, infinite on $K$ and finite at every point outside $K$. $\square$

title: 4.3.3 Boundary minimum principles with polar exceptions
search_title: Boundary minimum principles with polar exceptions
text: Theorem 4.3.4 . 09FD5942CD4F Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ be Greenian and let $u$ be superharmonic and bounded below on $\Omega $. Suppose $\liminf _{\Omega \ni x\to z}u(x)\ge \alpha $ for every boundary point outside a polar set $Z$. Then $u\ge \alpha $ if $d=2$, or if $\Omega $ is bounded. For an unbounded domain in dimension at least three the same conclusion holds provided $\liminf _{x\in \Omega ,|x|\to \infty }u(x)\ge \alpha $. Proof. For a bounded $\Omega $, a global polar function infinite on $Z$ can be made nonnegative on $\overline\Omega $ by adding a constant. Call it $v$. Then $u+\varepsilon v$ has boundary lower limits at least $\alpha $ at all points, including $Z$, since $u$ is bounded below. The bounded-domain minimum principle gives $u+\varepsilon v\ge \alpha $. Average over a small interior ball; its average of $v$ is finite. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and then the radius decrease to zero to obtain $u\ge \alpha $ everywhere. The case with a condition at infinity follows by truncating with large balls, using $u\ge \alpha -\eta $ outside such a ball, and then letting $\eta \downarrow 0$. We need one planar fact: the boundary of a nonempty Greenian open set is not polar. If $\Omega $ is not dense and its boundary were polar, take an entire superharmonic polar function $v$ infinite there and replace it by infinity on one component of $\Omega $. The result is lsc, locally supermean (the boundary values are infinity), finite somewhere in the open complement, and hence superharmonic on the plane. It cannot be infinity on a nonempty open set, a contradiction. If $\Omega $ is dense, its complement equals its boundary. A fixed-pole Green function is bounded away from its pole, so polar removability extends it harmonically across the complement outside a small pole ball. Its harmonic correction then extends to the whole plane, and the resulting nonnegative fundamental-plus-harmonic function contradicts the whole-plane nonexistence proved earlier. Thus the planar fact holds. For unbounded planar $\Omega $, choose $z_0\in \partial \Omega \setminus Z$. For any $\eta >0$ choose $r>0$ with $u\ge \alpha -\eta $ on $\Omega \cap \overline{B(z_0,r)}$. On $D=\Omega \setminus \overline{B(z_0,r)}$ the function $v(x)=\log (|x-z_0|/r)$ is nonnegative harmonic and tends to infinity at infinity. Since $u$ is bounded below, $u+\varepsilon v$ satisfies the required boundary inequality $\alpha -\eta $ on a sufficiently large outer sphere and on the inner sphere, and on the original boundary outside $Z$. The bounded-domain result gives $u+\varepsilon v\ge \alpha -\eta $ on every large truncation of $D$. Let the truncation grow, then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, then $\eta \downarrow 0$. Together with the inner ball inequality this proves the assertion on $\Omega $. $\square$

title: 4.3.5 Reduction and capacity on an admissible open set

For a nonnegative superharmonic $u$ on a Greenian open set $\Omega $, let $R_ Eu$ be the infimum of nonnegative superharmonic majorants of $u$ on $E\subset \Omega $, and let $\widehat R_ Eu$ be its lsc regularization. Call $\Omega $ admissible if its compactly supported Green potentials tend to zero at every finite boundary point outside a polar set. In dimension at least three they also tend to zero at infinity, by $G\le \Phi $. The results in this section assert this hypothesis explicitly; its eventual verification for every Greenian set belongs to the boundary theory. Theorem 4.3.6 . C651523E22C3 For any $E$, $0\le \widehat R_ Eu\le R_ Eu\le u$, and the regularized reduction is superharmonic. It equals $u$ on the interior of $E$, is harmonic and equal to $R_ Eu$ outside $\overline E$, and differs from $R_ Eu$ only on a polar subset of $\partial E$. Reductions preserve order in $E,u$, positive scaling, and subadditivity in $u$. If $K\Subset \Omega $ is compact, then $\widehat R_ Ku$ is a Green potential, without assuming $u$ bounded on $K$. Proof. The family of majorants is nonempty (it contains $u$), closed under minimum and locally bounded below. The checked Foundations subharmonic envelope and polar limit discrepancy , applied after sign reversal, give superharmonic regularization and a polar discrepancy set. On $E$ the unregularized infimum equals $u$, and locality gives equality of the regularization on the interior. Outside $\overline E$, the family is saturated under ball lowering, so its infimum is harmonic by Lemma 3.5.2 ; it is nonnegative, excluding $-\infty $. Order and scaling follow from the defining families. Sums of majorants majorize the sum; the unregularized inequality passes to regularizations almost everywhere by the polar discrepancy assertion, and then everywhere by ball-average representatives. For bounded $u$ on $K$, in each component meeting $K$ choose a pole $a$. A multiple of $G(a,\cdot )$ majorizes $u$ on that component's compact intersection with $K$, since its positive lsc kernel has a positive minimum there. On all other components use $u$. This competitor shows $\widehat R_ Ku\le C G(a,\cdot )$ on the chosen component, so it has zero greatest harmonic minorant there. Components disjoint from $K$ have zero reduction. The global Riesz theorem makes the reduction a potential. For general $u=p+h$ with $p$ a potential and $h\ge 0$ harmonic, $h$ is bounded on $K$. The reduction of $p$ is dominated by $p$, hence has zero harmonic minorant; that of $h$ is a potential by the bounded case. Subadditivity bounds the reduction of $u$ by their sum, so it too has zero minorant and is a potential. $\square$ Theorem 4.3.7 . ABDF7610F7B2 Suppose $\Omega $ is admissible. Moreover \[  C(K)=\sup \{ \mu (K):\operatorname {supp}\mu \subset K,\  G\mu \le 1\} .  \] Capacity is monotone, continuous along decreasing compact sets, and strongly subadditive. The inner/outer extension \[  C_*(A)=\sup _{K\subset A}C(K),\qquad C^*(A)=\inf _{O\supset A\  {m open}} C_*(O)  \] is a Choquet outer capacity: monotone, continuous on increasing sequences of arbitrary sets and on decreasing compact sets. Every K-analytic subset of $\Omega $, hence every Borel set, is capacitable. Its zero sets are exactly the polar sets. Proof. The reduction theorem proves the representation and, since $V_ K$ equals one on the interior and is harmonic outside $K$, its Riesz measure is supported on $\partial K$. If $p=G\mu \le 1$ is supported on $K$ and $v$ is admissible for $W_ K$, then $v-p$ is superharmonic and bounded below outside $K$. Its boundary lower limits are nonnegative: at $K$ use $v\ge 1$, at the ambient boundary use admissibility, outside a polar exception. At infinity use decay when required. Its potential $G\mu _ L=1$ on $K$. For measures $\mu ,

u \, d\mu _ L=
u (K)$. Taking $
u =\mu _ K$ proves the supremum formula and monotonicity. If $K_ j\downarrow K$, put $g=\lim W_{K_ j}$. Its regularization is a potential dominated by $V_{K_1}$, harmonic off $K$ by harmonic convergence, and at most one. The greatest-potential characterization bounds it by $V_ K$, while monotonicity bounds it below by $V_ K$. Hence $g=V_ K=W_ K$ off $K$, and all $W_{K_ j}=W_ K=1$ on $K$, proving $W_{K_ j}\downarrow W_ K$. For open sets strong subadditivity follows by decomposing each compact subset of their union into finitely many compact pieces in the respective opens, adding a compact subset of the intersection, and applying compact strong subadditivity. title: Theorem 4.3.6
text: Theorem 4.3.6 . C651523E22C3 For any $E$, $0\le \widehat R_ Eu\le R_ Eu\le u$, and the regularized reduction is superharmonic. It equals $u$ on the interior of $E$, is harmonic and equal to $R_ Eu$ outside $\overline E$, and differs from $R_ Eu$ only on a polar subset of $\partial E$. Reductions preserve order in $E,u$, positive scaling, and subadditivity in $u$. If $K\Subset \Omega $ is compact, then $\widehat R_ Ku$ is a Green potential, without assuming $u$ bounded on $K$. Proof. The family of majorants is nonempty (it contains $u$), closed under minimum and locally bounded below. The checked Foundations subharmonic envelope and polar limit discrepancy , applied after sign reversal, give superharmonic regularization and a polar discrepancy set. On $E$ the unregularized infimum equals $u$, and locality gives equality of the regularization on the interior. Outside $\overline E$, the family is saturated under ball lowering, so its infimum is harmonic by Lemma 3.5.2 ; it is nonnegative, excluding $-\infty $. Order and scaling follow from the defining families. Sums of majorants majorize the sum; the unregularized inequality passes to regularizations almost everywhere by the polar discrepancy assertion, and then everywhere by ball-average representatives. For bounded $u$ on $K$, in each component meeting $K$ choose a pole $a$. A multiple of $G(a,\cdot )$ majorizes $u$ on that component's compact intersection with $K$, since its positive lsc kernel has a positive minimum there. On all other components use $u$. This competitor shows $\widehat R_ Ku\le C G(a,\cdot )$ on the chosen component, so it has zero greatest harmonic minorant there. Components disjoint from $K$ have zero reduction. The global Riesz theorem makes the reduction a potential. For general $u=p+h$ with $p$ a potential and $h\ge 0$ harmonic, $h$ is bounded on $K$. The reduction of $p$ is dominated by $p$, hence has zero harmonic minorant; that of $h$ is a potential by the bounded case. Subadditivity bounds the reduction of $u$ by their sum, so it too has zero minorant and is a potential. $\square$

title: 3.5.15 A global extension finite outside a prescribed ball
search_title: A global extension finite outside a prescribed ball
text: Lemma 3.5.16 . 7C49056207BE If $u$ is superharmonic on $B(a,R)$ and $0<r<R$, there is an entire superharmonic function equal to $u$ on $B(a,r)$ and finite outside $\overline{B(a,r)}$. Proof. Shrink $R$ while keeping $r<R$, and subtract a lower bound so $u\ge 0$ on a neighborhood of the new closed ball. Reduce $u$ onto $K=\overline{B(a,r)}$ relative to $B(a,R)$. The regularized reduction $p$ equals $u$ inside $K$, is a potential with measure supported in $K$, and is harmonic outside $K$. Its measure is finite by compact support, so $p\to 0$ on the outer sphere. Harmonic reflection extends it to a slightly larger annulus; denote the extension again by $p$. Let $F(x)=\alpha (\Phi (x-a)-\Phi (Re_1))$. It is radial harmonic outside $a$ and zero on the outer sphere. The normal derivative of $\Phi $ is strictly negative there. Since $p$ is smooth on a compact collar of that sphere and zero on it, a sufficiently large $\alpha >0$ makes $F\ge p$ on the inner half of a thinner collar and $F\le p$ on its outer half: divide the radial differences by $|x-a|-R$ and use uniform continuity of the radial derivatives. Define $u^*=p$ inside the sphere and $u^*=F$ outside. In the collar it is the minimum of two harmonic functions, hence superharmonic, so locality proves it is entire superharmonic. It is finite outside $K$. Finally restore the subtracted constant. $\square$

title: 4.4.1 Perron solutions and completed harmonic measure
search_title: Perron solutions and completed harmonic measure
section: 4.4 Perron theory and fine boundary limits
text: Let $D$ be a nonempty bounded open set. For extended boundary data $f$, let $\mathcal U_ f$ consist of componentwise superharmonic or identically infinite functions bounded below on $D$ with boundary lower limits at least $f$. Put $\overline H_ f=\inf \mathcal U_ f$ and $\underline H_ f=-\overline H_{-f}$. A function is resolutive when these coincide and are finite harmonic on every component. Theorem 4.4.2 . 09873BDAF3E0 Upper and lower solutions are componentwise harmonic or identically one of the two infinities, and $\underline H_ f\le \overline H_ f$. Each continuous boundary function is resolutive. There are probability measures $\omega _ x$ on $\partial D$, completed simultaneously for all $x\in D$, such that $f$ is resolutive exactly when it is measurable in all these completions and $\int |f|d\omega _ x<\infty $ for every $x$; then $H_ f(x)=\int f d\omega _ x$. For nonnegative measurable data the upper and lower solutions both equal the integral, possibly infinity. Within each component the measures are mutually absolutely continuous, their $L^ p$ spaces and weak/strong topologies agree, $1\le p<\infty $, and their norms are equivalent. The map $x\mapsto \omega _ x$ is weakly continuous. Proof. The finite superharmonic members of an upper class form a nonempty saturated family whenever that class has a member finite somewhere in the component: minimum and ball lowering preserve the boundary inequalities and the lower bound. The saturated-family lemma gives its harmonic or $-\infty $ infimum; if there is no such member the infimum is infinity. For $u$ in the lower and $v$ in the upper class, $v-u$ is superharmonic, bounded below, with nonnegative boundary lower limits, including where $f=\pm \infty $ (use the global bounds to avoid undefined subtraction). The bounded minimum principle gives $u\le v$. Order, constant translation, positive scaling, sign reversal and upper subadditivity follow from the defining classes, whenever sums are defined. For finite resolutive functions these prove linearity. A uniform change of boundary data by at most $\varepsilon $ changes each solution by at most $\varepsilon $, hence uniform limits of resolutive data are resolutive. The checked Foundations perron resolutivity supplies equality of the continuous upper and lower subsolution envelopes for continuous $f$. These classes are contained in our classes, so their common harmonic value lies between our lower and upper solutions; the reverse inequalities from class inclusion force equality here. Equivalently, approximate continuous data by smooth functions and split each smooth function as a difference of continuous subharmonic functions by adding a large multiple of $|x|^2$. We supply the required monotone limit argument. If $f_ j\uparrow f$ and $\overline H_{f_1}>-\infty $, then $\overline H_{f_ j}\uparrow \overline H_ f$. Work on one component. If the limit is infinity, order proves the claim. Otherwise the limit $h$ is harmonic by monotone harmonic convergence. At a fixed $x_0$ choose $v_ j\in \mathcal U_{f_ j}$ with $v_ j(x_0)<\overline H_{f_ j}(x_0)+\varepsilon 2^{-j}$. The nonnegative superharmonic series \[  v=h+\sum _ j(v_ j-\overline H_{f_ j})  \] is finite at $x_0$, hence superharmonic, and dominates every $v_ j$. It is bounded below by one $v_ j$ and has boundary lower limits at least $f$, so belongs to $\mathcal U_ f$. Its value at $x_0$ is at most $h(x_0)+\varepsilon $. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; harmonicity and the minimum principle, or repetition at each $x_0$, gives the claim. The negative-data version gives the corresponding decreasing limit. If all $f_ j$ are resolutive, their increasing limit has equal upper/lower solutions, and is resolutive when the common value is finite. For continuous data, $f\mapsto H_ f(x)$ is positive linear, sends $1$ to $1$, and has norm one. Compact-space Riesz representation gives the unique probability $\omega _ x$. Decreasing continuous approximations to indicators of closed subsets, followed by the monotone limit just proved, give $H_{1_ F}(x)=\omega _ x(F)$ for closed $F$. The class of boundary sets for which this equality and resolutivity hold contains the closed sets, is closed under proper differences and increasing unions, and therefore contains their generated sigma algebra. For clarity, the elementary pi-lambda argument proves the last assertion: first fix a closed set and close the class of sets whose intersections with it lie in the class; then repeat with an arbitrary member. This gives closure under finite intersections, hence under finite unions and, with increasing unions, under all countable unions. Thus all Borel indicators, bounded simple functions, and by monotone approximation all nonnegative Borel functions have the integral formula. For a Borel null set $N$ at $x$, positivity and harmonicity show $H_{1_ N}=0$ on its component. Every subset of $N$ has upper and lower solutions zero there, by order. Thus the formula extends to the completion of $\omega _ x$, and componentwise to the intersection of all these completed sigma algebras. Simple approximation proves the nonnegative formula; positive/negative parts prove sufficiency for integrable data. A positive harmonic function is finite everywhere in a component if finite at one point, so integrability at one point per component suffices. For necessity suppose $f$ is resolutive and work on one component. Choose decreasing $v_ j\in \mathcal U_ f$ whose values at $x_0$ tend to $H_ f(x_0)$, and put $F_ j(z)=\liminf _{D\ni x\to z}v_ j(x)$. These are lower semicontinuous extended Borel functions, bounded below, decreasing and at least $f$. Their harmonic solutions satisfy $H_ f\le H_{F_ j}\le v_ j$; they are finite at $x_0$ and hence finite harmonic everywhere. Similarly lower-class approximants yield increasing Borel integrable $G_ j\le f$, with $H_{G_ j}(x_0)\to H_ f(x_0)$. Let $F=\inf F_ j$, $G=\sup G_ j$. The inequalities $G_1\le G\le f\le F\le F_1$ imply that $F,G$ are integrable for every $\omega _ x$. Monotone integration gives $\int (F-G)d\omega _{x_0}=0$. The nonnegative harmonic integral of $F-G$ is then zero throughout the component. Thus $F=f=G$ almost everywhere for every $\omega _ x$, proving completed measurability and integrability. Finally Harnack applied to $H_{1_ E}$ gives $C^{-1}\omega _ y(E)\le \omega _ x(E)\le C\omega _ y(E)$ for fixed interior $x,y$ in one component. Integration yields $C^{-1/p}\| f\| _{p,y}\le \| f\| _{p,x}\le C^{1/p}\| f\| _{p,y}$. Equivalent norms give the same continuous dual and weak topology; strong topologies also agree. These statements apply to the $p$th powers of norms, which are harmonic integrals; the norms themselves need not be harmonic. Weak continuity of measures follows since $\int f d\omega _ x=H_ f(x)$ is continuous for every continuous $f$. $\square$ Lemma 4.4.3 . 621606E7390C Changing any boundary data on a polar set leaves both Perron solutions unchanged. If $f$ is resolutive on a bounded $D$ and $W\subset D$ is open, the data equal to $H_ f$ on $D\cap \partial W$ and to $f$ on $\partial D\cap \partial W$ are resolutive on $W$, with solution $H_ f|_ W$. Proof. For any interior $a$, choose an entire superharmonic polar function infinite on the exceptional set and finite at $a$, adding a constant to make it nonnegative on $\overline D$. Add $\varepsilon $ times it to every upper competitor. This is a competitor for either set of boundary data; evaluation at $a$ and $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives equality. Negate for lower solutions. For restriction, an upper competitor dominates $H_ f$ in $D$, so its boundary lower limits on interior boundary points of $W$ dominate $H_ f$ by harmonic continuity; on the remaining points they dominate $f$. Thus the restricted upper solution is at most $H_ f$, while the lower solution is at least $H_ f$. Bounded-domain comparison forces equality. $\square$

text: Lemma 4.4.3 . 621606E7390C Changing any boundary data on a polar set leaves both Perron solutions unchanged. If $f$ is resolutive on a bounded $D$ and $W\subset D$ is open, the data equal to $H_ f$ on $D\cap \partial W$ and to $f$ on $\partial D\cap \partial W$ are resolutive on $W$, with solution $H_ f|_ W$. Proof. For any interior $a$, choose an entire superharmonic polar function infinite on the exceptional set and finite at $a$, adding a constant to make it nonnegative on $\overline D$. text: A weak local barrier at $a\in \partial D$ is a strictly positive superharmonic function near $a$ in $D$ tending to zero at $a$. Theorem 4.4.5 . 2F74CBABB2A6 For bounded open $D$, a weak local barrier exists exactly when $a$ is regular for continuous Perron data. In that case the harmonic solution $H_ m$ for $m(z)=|z-a|$ is a global barrier, satisfies $H_ m(x)\ge |x-a|$, and has positive infimum away from every neighborhood of $a$. At such a point the upper boundary limsup of $\overline H_ f$ is at most the boundary limsup of $f$ for bounded-above $f$, and the analogous lower inequality holds for bounded-below data. Bounded data continuous at $a$ therefore attain their value there. Proof. The convex function $|x-a|$ is subharmonic by Jensen on harmonic coordinate functions, so lies in the lower class for $m$. Thus $H_ m\ge |x-a|>0$. Let $w$ be a weak local barrier, and choose a small sphere of radius $r$ centered at $a$ within its domain. Put $M=\max _{\partial D}|z-a|$. Choose compact $F\subset D\cap \partial B(a,r)$ whose complement in that open spherical set has normalized area less than $r/M$; if the open set is empty no $F$ is needed and comparison directly gives $H_ m\le r$ inside. Otherwise $k=\inf _ Fw>0$ (if $F$ is empty choose it nonempty by taking a smaller error). Let $b$ be the ball Poisson integral of boundary data $M$ on $(D\cap \partial B)\setminus F$ and zero elsewhere. It is nonnegative, continuous near the center, with $b(a)<r$. For every lower competitor $v$ for $m$, bounded comparison on $D\cap B$ gives \[  v\le r+(M/k)w+b.  \] On $F$ the $w$ term dominates the bound $v\le M$; on the remaining open sphere the Poisson limit is $M$; on the original boundary $v$ has upper limit at most $m\le r$. These verify every boundary piece. Taking the supremum and then approaching $a$ gives $\limsup H_ m\le 2r$. Let $r\to 0$. The global barrier and its positive-away-from-$a$ lower bound now follow from $H_ m\ge |x-a|$. For bounded-above data with local limsup $L$, the function $L+\varepsilon +cH_ m$ belongs to the upper class when $c$ is large enough to control the data outside a small neighborhood. Its limit at $a$ is $L+\varepsilon $. The case $L=-\infty $ is handled with any finite upper target instead. Negation gives the lower inequality. Conversely, regularity applied to continuous $m$ makes $H_ m$ a weak barrier. $\square$ Theorem 4.4.6 . 123C9AB7C052 Boundary regularity is inherited by open subsets at a common boundary point. An exterior tangent ball or an exterior truncated solid cone gives regularity. A planar exterior segment also gives regularity. For an exterior ball tangent only at $a$ use minus its radial fundamental function after subtracting its value on the sphere; it is positive on the exterior and tends to zero at $a$. A smaller internally tangent ball removes other contact points. For a planar exterior segment choose the logarithm branch cut along its ray; on a sufficiently small slit ball $-\operatorname {Re}(1/\log (z-a))=-\log |z-a|/|\log (z-a)|^2$ is a positive harmonic barrier tending to zero. For a cone, shrink it and enlarge the domain locally to the truncated cone complement $D_\rho =B(a,\rho )\setminus C$. All its boundary points other than $a$ have exterior balls, hence are regular. On $D_{2\rho }$ let $u$ be the Perron solution for $|z-a|$. On the outer sphere it equals $2\rho $; on lateral cone boundary it equals $|z-a|$. It is bounded between zero and $2\rho $ and is strictly less than $2\rho $ inside. On the compact radius-$\rho $ spherical section (including its regular lateral endpoints) its maximum is $b<2\rho $. Choose $q$ with $\max \{ 1/2,b/(2\rho )\} <q<1$. On the boundary of $D_\rho $ except $a$, $u(x)\le q u(a+2(x-a))$: on the outer section use $b<q2\rho $ and on the lateral section use the factor two. The difference is bounded harmonic; the polar boundary minimum principle permits the singleton exception at $a$. The inequality holds inside. Its finite nonnegative limsup $L$ at $a$ satisfies $L\le qL$, hence is zero. This is a weak local barrier and proves cone regularity. For exhaustion we give details of the finite-ball construction. Cover any compact $K$ in the open set by finitely many balls of a common radius $r$, with centers in $K$ and closures still inside the open set; choose the cover so a small interval of larger common radii still covers $K$ and has closures inside. Avoid finitely many critical radii: at a boundary point of the union, if the active outward normals had zero in their convex hull, that point would be the circumcenter in the affine span of some affinely independent subset of at most $d+1$ centers, by a minimal convex representation. Each such subset has at most one circumradius, giving a finite forbidden list. At an allowed radius the convex hull of the active normals avoids zero. Its nearest point to zero gives a direction with strictly positive scalar product with every active normal. A small solid cone in this direction avoids all active balls; the other finitely many balls have a positive gap locally. title: 4.4.7 Green boundary limits, Kellogg's theorem and planar Greenian sets

section: 4.4 Perron theory and fine boundary limits
text: Theorem 4.4.8 . 52535FA416BF Every Greenian open set is admissible: one polar subset $Z$ of its finite boundary works for zero boundary limits of all compactly supported Green potentials. On a bounded connected open set a boundary point is regular exactly when a fixed interior-pole Green function tends to zero there. The irregular boundary points form a polar set. Bounded-density boundary limits hold with the same exception under the volume hypotheses of Theorem 3.5.12 . Proof. For a bounded open set, continuous boundary data $\Phi _ a$ have a finite harmonic Perron solution, and $G(a,\cdot )=\Phi _ a-H_{\Phi _ a}$. Indeed $\Phi _ a$ is an upper competitor, so the right side is nonnegative and admissible, hence at least $G$. Writing $G=\Phi _ a+h_ a$, the function $-h_ a$ is a lower competitor: it is bounded above by $\Phi _ a$ and bounded on a pole neighborhood by harmonicity, so bounded above throughout the bounded set. Its boundary upper limits are at most $\Phi _ a$. Thus $-h_ a\le H_{\Phi _ a}$, giving the opposite inequality. At regular points the formula gives zero boundary limit; conversely such a Green function is positive harmonic near a boundary point and supplies a weak local barrier. For arbitrary Greenian $\Omega $, exhaust by bounded regular open sets $D_ j\Subset \Omega $ containing a fixed pole $a$. Extend $G_{D_ j}(a,\cdot )$ by zero outside $D_ j$. On the complement of a small closed pole ball these are nonnegative continuous subharmonic functions: they are harmonic inside, zero outside, and at a boundary point their value zero is at most every sufficiently small sphere average. They increase to the zero extension $g$ of $G_\Omega (a,\cdot )$, bounded above there by the fixed-pole kernel bound. The checked subharmonic envelope/polar discrepancy theorem says $g=g^*$ outside a polar set. On $\partial \Omega $, $g=0$ and $g^*\ge \limsup _{\Omega \ni x\to z}G_\Omega (a,x)\ge 0$, so that limsup is zero off a polar set. Choose one pole in each component; there are at most countably many components. The union of their exceptions is polar. Harnack chains in the pole variable make the zero limit uniform on any compact subset of poles in a component. A compact subset meets only finitely many components, so the limit is uniform on every compact subset of $\Omega $. Integration against a finite compactly supported measure proves admissibility with one common exceptional set. The bounded-density statement is then precisely the compact-tail estimate already proved. On a bounded connected set, regularity and the fixed-pole condition are equivalent by the first part, so the irregular set is contained in that pole's polar exception. These arguments remove the temporary admissibility hypothesis in the capacity theorem without using that theorem to prove the boundary discrepancy. $\square$ Theorem 4.4.9 . 2C2E1569F3E2 For a nonempty planar open set $\Omega $, the following are equivalent: its complement is nonpolar; it supports a nonconstant strictly positive superharmonic function; and it has a Green function. Proof. A Greenian set has nonpolar boundary by the planar fact in the polar boundary minimum proof, hence nonpolar complement. Conversely, fix $a\in \Omega $. Countably many open disks tangent at $a$ cover the plane minus $a$. If the closed complement is nonpolar, one of its compact intersections $K$ with the corresponding closed disks is nonpolar. Take a larger tangent disk $B$ with $K\Subset B$ and $a\in \partial B$. The ball capacitary potential $p$ of $K$ is nonzero, lies in $[0,1]$, is harmonic off $K$ and zero at $\partial B$. Extend it by zero outside $B$. This is continuous subharmonic on the complement of $K$, by the same boundary mean argument as above. Then $2-p$ is strictly positive superharmonic on $\Omega $ and nonconstant near $a$: it equals two on the outer side of $\partial B$ and is strictly smaller on the adjacent inner component. This formulation also works if $B\setminus K$ has other components where $p=1$. It remains to obtain a Green kernel from a nonconstant positive superharmonic function $s$, first when $\Omega $ is connected. For any pole $a$, the strong minimum principle gives $b$ with $s(b)<s(a)$. Scale and truncate $s$ so it is at least one on a small closed ball $\overline{B(a,r)}$ and less than one at $b$. The regularized infimum $v$ of nonnegative superharmonic majorants of one on that ball lies in $[0,1]$, equals one inside, is harmonic outside, and is less than one at $b$; these use only saturated families and the checked polar discrepancy theorem, not a Green kernel on $\Omega $. It is continuous on the inner sphere: on a slightly larger concentric annulus its boundary values are continuous on the outer sphere, one on the inner sphere outside a polar exception; Perron comparison ignoring that exception and annulus regularity give inner limit one. Thus $w=1-v$ is continuous subharmonic, zero on the ball, and strictly positive on its complement. That complement is connected: any path crossing the ball may be detoured through a slightly larger sphere inside $\Omega $. Choose $t>r$ with $\overline{B(a,t)}\subset \Omega $, and $2\alpha =\min _{|x-a|=t}w(x)>0$. Define a subharmonic $q$ by $\log (|x-a|/r)$ on the inner ball, by $\max \{ \log (|x-a|/r),(w(x)/\alpha )\log (t/r)\} $ on the annulus, and by the second term outside the radius-$t$ ball. At the inner sphere the extension dominates the harmonic logarithm with the same value; its sphere submeans follow. Near the outer sphere the second term dominates strictly, so locality proves subharmonicity. It is bounded above and $q+\Phi _ a=-\log r$ near $a$. If $C$ bounds $q$, the nonnegative superharmonic function $C-q$ is $\Phi _ a$ plus a superharmonic correction extending across $a$. Thus the admissible class $\mathcal B_ a$ is nonempty, and the minimal-kernel construction gives a Green function. A disconnected planar open set is already Greenian by the earlier component construction, so the connected argument suffices. $\square$
