text: Theorem 4.3.9 . 39A7F7684147 On a Greenian $\Omega $, a polar set $Z$ has a strictly positive superharmonic pole function finite at any prescribed $a\notin Z$. Consequently $R_ Eu=\widehat R_ Eu$ outside $E$, removing a polar subset from $E$ does not change the regularized reduction, and for increasing relatively closed $F_ j$ with union $F$, $\widehat R_{F_ j}u\uparrow \widehat R_ Fu$. For $W\Subset \Omega $ open, \[  \widehat R_{\Omega \setminus W}u=H^ W_{u|_{\partial W}}\quad \hbox{on }W.  \] For such $W$ the reduction is additive in $u$. Along an increasing exhaustion $W_ j$, these interior harmonic functions decrease to the greatest harmonic minorant of $u$, and their limit is zero exactly when $u$ is a potential. Proof. Work componentwise, choosing the prescribed point in its component and an arbitrary point in every other component outside the polar set. Cover $Z$ in the component by countably many small closed interior balls avoiding that point. The checked bounded-polar globalization with compact cutoffs gives finite measures supported in these balls, whose fundamental potentials are infinite on the covered polar pieces. Their Green potentials have the same poles by the local harmonic-correction identity, and are finite at the chosen point. Weight them so the sum of their masses and their potentials at that point is finite. The sum is a Green potential finite there and infinite on $Z$. Add the constant one for strict positivity, and glue the componentwise functions; superharmonicity is local. The discrepancy between $R_ Eu$ and its regularization is polar. For $a\notin E$ choose the pole function $p$ for its discrepancy on $E$, finite at $a$. Then $\widehat R_ Eu+\varepsilon p$ is a majorant of $u$ on $E$; evaluating at $a$ and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves equality there. If a polar subset is removed from $E$, adding its $\varepsilon $-pole function to any majorant on the remainder proves the opposite inequality almost everywhere; ball averages make it hold for the regularizations everywhere. For increasing $F_ j$, their increasing regularized reductions have a superharmonic limit $v\le \widehat R_ Fu$. On each $F_ j$ they equal $u$ outside a polar set; the union of these exceptions is polar. Thus $v$ majorizes $u$ on $F$ outside a polar set, and the polar-removal argument gives $v\ge \widehat R_ Fu$. Put $h=H^ W_ u$, which is finite harmonic because $0\le h\le u$ on $W$, and set $v=h$ on $W$, $v=u$ elsewhere. We justify the pasting even if $u$ has infinite boundary values. For any ball $B\Subset \Omega $, positivity of Perron solutions gives $H^ B_ v\le H^ B_ u\le u$ on $B\setminus W$. On $B\cap W$, compare the boundary values of $H^ B_ v$ and $v$, using the restriction lemma first from $B$ and then from $W$; both domains involved are bounded. This gives $H^ B_ v\le v$ there as well. If $\widehat v$ is the lsc regularization, $H^ B_{\widehat v}\le H^ B_ v\le v$; its harmonic continuity then gives $H^ B_{\widehat v}\le \widehat v$. The ball comparison characterization proves $\widehat v$ superharmonic. On $\partial W$, approximate the lsc boundary function $u$ increasingly by continuous functions. At regular points of $W$, their Perron solutions have the prescribed limits, so $\liminf _ W h\ge u$ there. The irregular set is polar. Hence $\widehat v\ge u$ on $\Omega \setminus W$ outside a polar set, proving $\widehat v\ge \widehat R_{\Omega \setminus W}u$. Conversely any defining majorant is in the upper Perron class for $u$ on $W$, so dominates $v$; regularization gives the reverse inequality. On $W$, $\widehat v=v=h$, proving the formula. If $w\ge 0$ is superharmonic and $w\ge p$ on $\operatorname {supp}\mu $ except for a polar set, then $w\ge p$ throughout $\Omega $. Proof. The polar boundary minimum theorem gives $w\ge p$ off $K$; the inequality holds almost everywhere everywhere, and canonical ball averages give it at every point. To obtain them, apply Lusin to each residual potential, choose a compact subset of the residual carrier with arbitrarily small residual mass, and use the support-continuity principle; repeat with errors $2^{-j}$. Finally exhaust the support of a general Radon measure by increasing compact subsets. Each restriction has finite potential dominated by $p$, so the compact case applies. title: Theorem 4.3.9
text: Theorem 4.3.9 . 39A7F7684147 On a Greenian $\Omega $, a polar set $Z$ has a strictly positive superharmonic pole function finite at any prescribed $a\notin Z$. Consequently $R_ Eu=\widehat R_ Eu$ outside $E$, removing a polar subset from $E$ does not change the regularized reduction, and for increasing relatively closed $F_ j$ with union $F$, $\widehat R_{F_ j}u\uparrow \widehat R_ Fu$. For $W\Subset \Omega $ open, \[  \widehat R_{\Omega \setminus W}u=H^ W_{u|_{\partial W}}\quad \hbox{on }W.  \] For such $W$ the reduction is additive in $u$. Along an increasing exhaustion $W_ j$, these interior harmonic functions decrease to the greatest harmonic minorant of $u$, and their limit is zero exactly when $u$ is a potential. Proof. Work componentwise, choosing the prescribed point in its component and an arbitrary point in every other component outside the polar set. Cover $Z$ in the component by countably many small closed interior balls avoiding that point. The checked bounded-polar globalization with compact cutoffs gives finite measures supported in these balls, whose fundamental potentials are infinite on the covered polar pieces. Their Green potentials have the same poles by the local harmonic-correction identity, and are finite at the chosen point. Weight them so the sum of their masses and their potentials at that point is finite. The sum is a Green potential finite there and infinite on $Z$. Add the constant one for strict positivity, and glue the componentwise functions; superharmonicity is local. The discrepancy between $R_ Eu$ and its regularization is polar. For $a\notin E$ choose the pole function $p$ for its discrepancy on $E$, finite at $a$. Then $\widehat R_ Eu+\varepsilon p$ is a majorant of $u$ on $E$; evaluating at $a$ and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves equality there. If a polar subset is removed from $E$, adding its $\varepsilon $-pole function to any majorant on the remainder proves the opposite inequality almost everywhere; ball averages make it hold for the regularizations everywhere. For increasing $F_ j$, their increasing regularized reductions have a superharmonic limit $v\le \widehat R_ Fu$. On each $F_ j$ they equal $u$ outside a polar set; the union of these exceptions is polar. Thus $v$ majorizes $u$ on $F$ outside a polar set, and the polar-removal argument gives $v\ge \widehat R_ Fu$. Put $h=H^ W_ u$, which is finite harmonic because $0\le h\le u$ on $W$, and set $v=h$ on $W$, $v=u$ elsewhere. We justify the pasting even if $u$ has infinite boundary values. For any ball $B\Subset \Omega $, positivity of Perron solutions gives $H^ B_ v\le H^ B_ u\le u$ on $B\setminus W$. On $B\cap W$, compare the boundary values of $H^ B_ v$ and $v$, using the restriction lemma first from $B$ and then from $W$; both domains involved are bounded. This gives $H^ B_ v\le v$ there as well. If $\widehat v$ is the lsc regularization, $H^ B_{\widehat v}\le H^ B_ v\le v$; its harmonic continuity then gives $H^ B_{\widehat v}\le \widehat v$. The ball comparison characterization proves $\widehat v$ superharmonic. On $\partial W$, approximate the lsc boundary function $u$ increasingly by continuous functions. At regular points of $W$, their Perron solutions have the prescribed limits, so $\liminf _ W h\ge u$ there. The irregular set is polar. Hence $\widehat v\ge u$ on $\Omega \setminus W$ outside a polar set, proving $\widehat v\ge \widehat R_{\Omega \setminus W}u$. Conversely any defining majorant is in the upper Perron class for $u$ on $W$, so dominates $v$; regularization gives the reverse inequality. On $W$, $\widehat v=v=h$, proving the formula. Linearity of integrable boundary solutions proves additivity inside $W$; outside $W$, both reductions equal the original function off a polar set. Ball averages remove that exception from the additive identity. In an exhaustion the reductions decrease by set order. Their interior harmonic limit is nonnegative and at most $u$. Every global harmonic minorant of $u$ is a lower Perron competitor on each $W_ j$, since it is continuous near $\partial W_ j$; it is therefore at most this limit. This identifies the greatest harmonic minorant. The zero characterization is the global Riesz theorem. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.3.10
text: Theorem 4.3.10 . C4F5D8B270EB Let $p=G_\Omega \mu $ be finite everywhere on a Greenian open set. If $w\ge 0$ is superharmonic and $w\ge p$ on $\operatorname {supp}\mu $ except for a polar set, then $w\ge p$ throughout $\Omega $. Proof. First let $\mu $ have compact support $K$ and $p$ be continuous. It is bounded on a compact neighborhood of $K$ and bounded outside it by the fixed-pole/Harnack bound, hence globally bounded. On $\Omega \setminus K$, $w-p$ is superharmonic and bounded below. At $K$ its lower boundary limits are nonnegative outside the stated polar exception by continuity of $p$ and lsc of $w$. At the ambient boundary the same holds because compact potentials tend to zero outside a polar set. If $d\ge 3$, at infinity $p\to 0$. The polar boundary minimum theorem gives $w\ge p$ off $K$; the inequality holds almost everywhere everywhere, and canonical ball averages give it at every point. For general compactly supported $\mu $, the finite potential permits the Lusin construction of pairwise disjoint compact restrictions $\mu _ j$ with continuous potentials and $\mu =\sum \mu _ j$. To obtain them, apply Lusin to each residual potential, choose a compact subset of the residual carrier with arbitrarily small residual mass, and use the support-continuity principle; repeat with errors $2^{-j}$. The sum of the first $j$ restrictions has continuous potential, is dominated by $p$ on $K$, and therefore by $w$ everywhere by the first case. Nonnegative monotone convergence gives $p\le w$. Finally exhaust the support of a general Radon measure by increasing compact subsets. Each restriction has finite potential dominated by $p$, so the compact case applies. Monotone convergence finishes the proof. No convergence of signed differences at infinite values is used. $\square$

title: 4.4.10 Exterior Poisson kernels and Helms's point at infinity
search_title: Exterior Poisson kernels and Helms's point at infinity
section: 4.4 Perron theory and fine boundary limits
text: Let $\widehat{\mathbb R^ d}=\mathbb R^ d\cup \{ \infty \} $ have the one-point compactification topology. We use Helms's convention: superharmonicity at an interior infinity means lower semicontinuity there and $u(\infty )\ge M_{\partial B}u$ for every ball whose closed exterior lies in the domain. Harmonicity means the corresponding equality and both semicontinuities, in addition to ordinary harmonicity at finite points. This extra mean condition is part of the definition, and is not implied by ordinary bounded exterior harmonicity in dimension at least three. Theorem 4.4.11 . E16C09608A00 Let $B=B(a,R)$ and let $f\in L^1(\partial B,d\sigma )$. Put $m=(s_{d-1}R^{d-1})^{-1}\int f d\sigma $ and $r=|x-a|$. The exterior solution in this compactified convention is \[  H^{\rm ext}_ Bf(x)=\frac1{s_{d-1}R}\int _{\partial B} \left[\frac{r^2-R^2}{|x-z|^ d}+\frac1{R^{d-2}}-\frac1{r^{d-2}}\right] f(z)d\sigma (z),\qquad r>R,  \] with $H^{\rm ext}_ Bf(\infty )=m$. It is harmonic including at infinity, positive when $f\ge 0$, sends one to one, and tends to $f$ at every continuity point of $f$ on the sphere. More generally an ordinary exterior harmonic $h$, continuous to the sphere with finite limit $\alpha $ at infinity, satisfies \[  h(x)=K\bigl (H_ B(h|_{\partial B})\bigr )(x) +\alpha \bigl [1-(R/r)^{d-2}\bigr ].  \] For $d=2$ necessarily $\alpha =m$; for $d\ge 3$, it is harmonic in Helms's sense at infinity exactly when $\alpha =m$. Proof. Invert about the sphere and apply Kelvin covariance. For $d\ge 3$, the Kelvin transform of bounded $h$ is bounded in absolute value by a multiple of the fundamental pole near $a$. Adding a sufficiently large multiple of that pole makes it nonnegative, so the proved Bôcher lemma applies. Its singular coefficient is $\alpha R^{d-2}$, by taking the limit back at infinity. Subtracting this singularity leaves a harmonic function on $B$; its continuous boundary data identify it by the ball Poisson formula, giving the displayed representation. In dimension two the Kelvin transform is bounded near the center and extends harmonically there, with center value $\alpha =m$. For integrable $f$, define the right side with $\alpha =m$. The inverted ball Poisson integral is harmonic away from $a$ and its derivatives are controlled on compact subsets by the integrable boundary density. The inversion distance identity gives precisely the displayed kernel. Its first term is positive; for $d\ge 3$ so is the correction $R^{2-d}-r^{2-d}$, and for $d=2$ that correction is zero. Evaluating at $f=1$ shows the total kernel mass is one. Its limit at infinity is $m$, and the ball Poisson continuity-point estimate, together with the vanishing correction at $r=R$, proves the boundary assertion. The Kelvin identity for concentric spherical means gives, for a general finite-limit $h$, \[  M_{\partial B(a,t)}h=\alpha +(m-\alpha )(R/t)^{d-2}\quad (d\ge 3),  \] and the constant $m$ if $d=2$. For the chosen $\alpha =m$ these means are constant, so their radial flux is zero. The divergence theorem on the region between any large sphere containing $\overline B$ and a larger concentric sphere transfers this zero flux to the arbitrary sphere. The annular mean derivative formula then makes its subsequent spherical means constant; their limit is the limit at infinity, namely $m$. Thus every exterior-ball mean equals $h(\infty )$, as required. Conversely Helms's mean condition for the concentric spheres forces $\alpha =m$. $\square$ Theorem 4.4.12 . 8FA95EB71F47 On a connected compactified open set a superharmonic function attaining its infimum is constant. On a proper open subset, nonnegative boundary lower limits imply nonnegativity. Entire superharmonic functions on $\widehat{\mathbb R^ d}$ are constant. Positive scaling, sums and minima preserve superharmonicity. Harmonic lowering is valid on interior balls and on exterior balls, directed harmonic convergence holds, and a nonempty saturated family under both kinds of lowering has harmonic or $-\infty $ infimum on each component. The point infinity is polar for $d=2$ and is not polar for $d\ge 3$. Proof. At finite points the minimum-set argument is the checked Euclidean one. If the minimum is attained at infinity, each large sphere mean is at least the minimum and at most the value there. Lower semicontinuity and positivity of the surface measure of open patches force equality at every point of each such sphere. Thus the minimum set contains an exterior neighborhood and is open and closed. For a proper open set each component has a nonempty boundary in the connected compact ambient space. Extend by boundary liminf; compactness forces a negative minimum to be attained inside if any negative value exists. The strong minimum principle would make the component a negative constant, contradicting its nonnegative boundary limits. For the entire compact space a minimum is attained and the function is constant; one cannot infer a nonnegative constant from an empty boundary. For algebraic operations use the ordinary local result and the linear sphere inequalities at infinity; nontriviality follows from finite almost everywhere values on each Euclidean component. For exterior lowering, increasing continuous minorants of the lsc sphere data and the positive exterior Poisson kernel give a harmonic minorant bounded above by $u$ via compactified comparison. Finite interior values exclude an infinite limit. The same boundary-liminf/pasting proof as for interior lowering makes the replacement superharmonic at finite points. Near infinity it is the exterior harmonic solution with constant large-sphere means equal to its value there. For every other allowed sphere center, the finite-point superharmonic mean is concave as a function of $r^{2-d}$ (or $-\log r$ in the plane), and is constant at that value for all sufficiently large radii, by the zero-flux argument above. Concavity bounds its earlier means by the same value, giving the required inequality at infinity. Directed harmonic limits reduce to the Euclidean result away from infinity and the positive exterior kernel on a fixed sphere near infinity; directed monotone integration identifies the value and harmonicity there. The saturated-family proof then applies in both kinds of neighborhoods, exactly as for finite balls, with nonemptiness explicitly required. For $d=2$, $\log |x-a|$ on an exterior neighborhood, with value infinity at infinity, is a superharmonic pole function there. For $d\ge 3$, concentric sphere means of a superharmonic function on an exterior are finite and concave functions of $t=r^{2-d}$. A supporting affine upper bound at an interior $t$ bounds them above as $t\downarrow 0$. If the value at infinity were infinite, lsc would instead force all sufficiently distant sphere means to tend to infinity. This contradiction proves nonpolarity. $\square$ Lemma 4.4.13 . 58BE7FB3C948 Kelvin transformation preserves superharmonicity on domains avoiding its center. If $u$ is superharmonic on $B(a,R)$, harmonic near $a$, and $u(a)=0$, its Kelvin transform, extended by zero at infinity, is superharmonic on the compactified exterior. Proof. On compact subdomains avoiding the center, transform harmonic comparison functions, use positivity of the Kelvin multiplier and its involutivity, and transform the comparison back. This proves the superharmonic comparison property for the transformed lsc function. In the normalized case the transform is harmonic near infinity with zero large-sphere means: the original function is harmonic near $a$ with zero center value, so the concentric mean identity and the flux transfer in the exterior theorem apply. In particular its value at infinity is zero and it is continuous there. For any other exterior ball in the domain, its sphere means are concave in $r^{2-d}$ (or $-\log r$ in the plane), and are zero for all sufficiently large radii. Concavity makes them nonpositive at the smaller allowed radii. This is exactly the supermean condition at infinity. $\square$

title: 4.4.14 Perron theory on the one-point compactification
search_title: Perron theory on the one-point compactification
section: 4.4 Perron theory and fine boundary limits
text: All domains in this section are proper open subsets of $\widehat{\mathbb R^ d}$ with nonpolar complement; harmonicity at an interior infinity has the exterior mean condition of the preceding section. Boundary limits and continuous data refer to this compactification. The upper class consists of bounded-below hyperharmonic functions whose boundary lower limits majorize the datum; lower classes are defined by sign reversal. We first construct the needed global pole functions, rather than presupposing their existence in a barrier argument. Lemma 4.4.15 . E0D6C3CD3750 If $\widehat{\mathbb R^ d}\setminus \overline\Omega $ is nonempty, continuous boundary data are resolutive. Every polar boundary set has a positive superharmonic blow-up function on $\Omega $. It can be chosen finite at any prescribed interior point. A finite boundary point is regular exactly when it admits a local weak barrier; the irregular set is polar. Infinity is always regular in $d\ge 3$ when it is a boundary point. Proof. Choose a closed ball disjoint from $\overline\Omega $ and invert about its sphere, sending $\Omega $ into a bounded ball. Continuous data, after subtracting a constant and a uniform approximation if necessary, can be assumed zero near infinity. The transformed data, divided by the positive Kelvin multiplier, then extend continuously with value zero near the inversion center. If infinity is interior, the center is separated from the transformed boundary and the same prescription is possible. Approximate uniformly by smooth functions $\varphi $ zero near that center. Such smooth approximation follows by extending a continuous function from the compact boundary, multiplying by a cutoff, and convolving; the uniform error on the boundary is controlled by uniform continuity. These approximants are differences of superharmonic functions harmonic and zero near the center. To verify this, take $q(x)=-A(|x-a|-r_0)_+^4$, with the support of $\Delta \varphi $ separated from $\overline{B(a,r_0)}$. Its Laplacian is nonpositive and strictly negative on that support; sufficiently large $A$ makes both $q$ and $\varphi +q$ superharmonic. Their normalized Kelvin transforms are superharmonic even at interior infinity by the normalized Kelvin lemma. On the exterior ball the Kelvin multiplier is bounded by one (it is one in the plane), so uniform approximation survives. Each transformed approximant is a difference of bounded superharmonic traces on a compact neighborhood of $\overline\Omega $; bounded subharmonic trace resolutivity, proved by comparing its lower solution with the upper class, applies with the compactified minimum principle. Uniform stability of the Perron classes proves continuous-data resolutivity. Positive-functional representation gives a probability harmonic measure on the compact boundary, including when the pole is infinity. For a polar boundary set, transform its finite points into the bounded ball and split it into countably many closed shells avoiding the center. The prescribed-point polar construction gives positive superharmonic pole functions finite at the center and at the chosen transformed interior point. Lower each harmonically on a sufficiently small center ball, which avoids that shell, and subtract its center value. Its normalized Kelvin transform is superharmonic at infinity and has the same required boundary blow-up. It is defined on a neighborhood of the compact exterior, and hence has a finite lower bound there by lower semicontinuity. Add a constant to make it positive. Choose summable positive coefficients giving a finite sum at the prescribed point (and at infinity if interior). Their sum is the required function. In dimension two, if the polar set contains infinity, add a positive multiple of $\log (|x-a|/R)$ on the exterior. In higher dimensions infinity cannot belong to a polar set. The same construction on a finite boundary singleton and epsilon comparison shows that its harmonic measure is zero. A local finite-point weak barrier can be upgraded on the bounded set $D=\Omega \cap B(a,r)$ by the proved bounded-domain weak-barrier theorem. Its strong barrier $g$ has a positive lower bound away from $a$. On a cutting sphere inside $B(a,r)$ choose $c>0$ below that lower bound; paste $\min (g,c)$ inside to the constant $c$ outside. They agree on a collar, so the pasted function is superharmonic, vanishes at $a$, and is bounded away from zero off every neighborhood of $a$. If infinity is interior, its value $c$ dominates every exterior sphere mean, since it is globally at most $c$. Thus the pasting remains valid there. The usual upper/lower barrier comparison proves regularity. Conversely use a bounded continuous boundary function $m\ge 0$ vanishing only at $a$. Its harmonic solution is positive on every component: otherwise its probability harmonic measure would be concentrated on the zero-mass singleton. At a regular point it tends to zero, giving a weak barrier. This avoids unbounded distance data on a boundary containing infinity. For a boundary infinity in $d\ge 3$, the fundamental function with any fixed finite pole is an explicit local weak barrier, positive and bounded away from zero on every bounded portion away from infinity. In dimension two inversion has multiplier one and transfers the finite-point local barrier criterion. At all finite points inversion preserves weak barriers locally. Thus the bounded-domain Kellogg theorem transfers to the inverted domain; polar sets transfer by Kelvin transformation. In $d\ge 3$ the possible extra center corresponds to an already regular infinity. This proves polar irregularity in all cases under the present nondensity hypothesis. $\square$ Lemma 4.4.16 . 5D12CB9707B5 On every proper domain with nonpolar complement a polar boundary set has a positive superharmonic blow-up function, finite at a prescribed interior point. A bounded harmonic function with zero boundary limits outside a polar set is zero. Proof. Only the dense case remains. Work in a connected component, choose $a\in \Omega $, and concentric closed balls with $0<r_0<r_1<r_2<r_3$, all contained in $\Omega $. Removing the smallest ball gives a nondense domain. Its pole function $v$ can be harmonically lowered on the annulus $r_0<|x-a|<r_3$, so it is finite harmonic near the two middle spheres. This preserves its true-boundary blow-up and positivity. Write $O=\Omega \setminus \overline{B(a,r_1)}$. This set is connected: any path in $\Omega $ entering the removed ball can be rerouted through the contained annulus. The harmonic measure $Q$ of its inner sphere is strictly below one on $O$. Indeed the original nonpolar boundary contains a regular point, since the nondense Kellogg exception is polar; $Q$ tends to zero there. The strong maximum principle then gives $q=\max _{|x-a|=r_2}Q(x)<1$. Set $w_0=0$. Given $w_{j-1}$, let $u_ j$ be the ball solution in $B(a,r_2)$ with data $v+w_{j-1}$ on its sphere. Let $w_ j$ be the bounded solution on $O$ with data $u_ j-v$ on the inner sphere and zero on the true boundary. These are continuous boundary data on the nondense domain. For consecutive differences the ball maximum principle and the bound by $Q$ give \[  \| u_{j+1}-u_ j\| _{S_{r_1}} \le \| w_ j-w_{j-1}\| _{S_{r_2}},\qquad \| w_{j+1}-w_ j\| _{S_{r_2}} \le q\| u_{j+1}-u_ j\| _{S_{r_1}}.  \] Thus the corrections converge in geometric series, uniformly on the respective boundaries and hence throughout their domains. Their limits $u,w$ are harmonic; $w$ is bounded. On both annulus boundary spheres, $u=v+w$, so annular uniqueness gives this equality throughout the overlap. Paste $u$ inside to $v+w$ outside. The result is superharmonic, harmonic near $a$, bounded below, and has the same polar boundary blow-up as $v$. Adding a constant makes it positive. This proves the assertion including finiteness at the prescribed center. Componentwise construction proves the disconnected version. For bounded harmonic $h$ with zero boundary limits outside a polar $Z$, compare $\pm h+\varepsilon p$ with zero, where $p$ is the positive blow-up function, finite at a prescribed interior point. Compactified boundary comparison applies even on $Z$, and yields $|h(a)|\le \varepsilon p(a)$. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and choose $a$ arbitrarily. The same epsilon argument permits polar exceptions in bounded Perron competitors. $\square$ Theorem 4.4.17 . A7E357C38C8E On every proper compactified domain with nonpolar complement, continuous boundary data are resolutive, the irregular boundary points form a polar set, and bounded harmonic solutions are unique with polar boundary exceptions. The integral characterization of resolutive data holds: an extended function is resolutive exactly when it is integrable for the simultaneously completed harmonic measures, and then $H_ f(x)=\int f\, d\omega _ x$. Polar boundary sets have zero harmonic measure. Proof. For a dense domain remove an interior closed ball. Solve the continuous datum $f$ on the true boundary and the constant $M+1$ on the artificial sphere, where $|f|\le M$. Paste $M+1$ inside by taking the minimum with that constant on a collar. The resulting bounded superharmonic function is a global upper competitor. The lower construction uses $-M-1$. At every regular true boundary point of the punctured nondense domain, these give the corresponding boundary limits for the global upper/lower solutions. Their difference is bounded harmonic, with zero boundary limits outside the polar Kellogg set, and is zero by the preceding lemma. Thus $f$ is resolutive. Those same upper/lower bounds show each such punctured-domain regular point is regular for $\Omega $, proving Kellogg for the general domain. Local barriers and the capped-constant construction give the equivalent local criterion as before. The full measurable-data proof now uses precisely the steps established for bounded domains: closed boundary indicators by continuous decreasing approximation, the pi-lambda argument, nonnegative simple approximation, and monotone continuity of the upper envelope via summable positive errors at a fixed pole. The only local harmonic operations needed are lowering and monotone convergence, available for both interior and exterior balls. For clarity, the necessity step also survives unchanged: countably many upper/lower competitors approximating a finite solution at a pole give Borel boundary liminf/limsup sandwiches. Their integrals have the same value at that pole, so their difference is zero almost everywhere there; positive harmonicity and Harnack transfer this common null set throughout the component. The sandwiches identify the datum in the completed measure class and give its absolute integrability. Conversely positive and negative integrable parts follow from monotone simple functions, and null changes are removed by the sandwich comparison. Apply this separately in the countably many components. Epsilon comparison with the constructed pole functions proves polar boundary nullity. This establishes the same full equivalence as the bounded Perron theorem, now with the compactified boundary condition at infinity included explicitly. $\square$ Theorem 4.4.18 . C07BA2371FA3 Let $F$ be relatively closed in a Euclidean Greenian $\Omega $, and let $u\ge 0$ be superharmonic. On $\partial (\Omega \setminus F)$ prescribe $u$ on the interior boundary and zero on the original compactified boundary. Call this nonnegative lsc datum $u_0$. Its Perron solution is finite harmonic on $\Omega \setminus F$, and \[  \widehat R_ Fu=H_{u_0}\quad \hbox{on }\Omega \setminus F.  \] On $F$ it equals $u$ except possibly at irregular interior boundary points, a polar set. For relatively closed $F$, sweeping is additive in $u$. Proof. The integral solution is bounded above by $u$, which is an upper competitor, and so is finite almost everywhere in each component. Positive harmonic alternatives make it finite everywhere there. Paste $H_{u_0}$ off $F$ to $u$ on $F$ and regularize. title: Lemma 4.4.15
section: 4.4 Perron theory and fine boundary limits
text: Lemma 4.4.15 . E0D6C3CD3750 If $\widehat{\mathbb R^ d}\setminus \overline\Omega $ is nonempty, continuous boundary data are resolutive. Every polar boundary set has a positive superharmonic blow-up function on $\Omega $. It can be chosen finite at any prescribed interior point. A finite boundary point is regular exactly when it admits a local weak barrier; the irregular set is polar. Infinity is always regular in $d\ge 3$ when it is a boundary point. Proof. Choose a closed ball disjoint from $\overline\Omega $ and invert about its sphere, sending $\Omega $ into a bounded ball. Continuous data, after subtracting a constant and a uniform approximation if necessary, can be assumed zero near infinity. The transformed data, divided by the positive Kelvin multiplier, then extend continuously with value zero near the inversion center. If infinity is interior, the center is separated from the transformed boundary and the same prescription is possible. Approximate uniformly by smooth functions $\varphi $ zero near that center. Such smooth approximation follows by extending a continuous function from the compact boundary, multiplying by a cutoff, and convolving; the uniform error on the boundary is controlled by uniform continuity. These approximants are differences of superharmonic functions harmonic and zero near the center. To verify this, take $q(x)=-A(|x-a|-r_0)_+^4$, with the support of $\Delta \varphi $ separated from $\overline{B(a,r_0)}$. Its Laplacian is nonpositive and strictly negative on that support; sufficiently large $A$ makes both $q$ and $\varphi +q$ superharmonic. Their normalized Kelvin transforms are superharmonic even at interior infinity by the normalized Kelvin lemma. On the exterior ball the Kelvin multiplier is bounded by one (it is one in the plane), so uniform approximation survives. Each transformed approximant is a difference of bounded superharmonic traces on a compact neighborhood of $\overline\Omega $; bounded subharmonic trace resolutivity, proved by comparing its lower solution with the upper class, applies with the compactified minimum principle. Uniform stability of the Perron classes proves continuous-data resolutivity. Positive-functional representation gives a probability harmonic measure on the compact boundary, including when the pole is infinity. For a polar boundary set, transform its finite points into the bounded ball and split it into countably many closed shells avoiding the center. The prescribed-point polar construction gives positive superharmonic pole functions finite at the center and at the chosen transformed interior point. Lower each harmonically on a sufficiently small center ball, which avoids that shell, and subtract its center value. Its normalized Kelvin transform is superharmonic at infinity and has the same required boundary blow-up. It is defined on a neighborhood of the compact exterior, and hence has a finite lower bound there by lower semicontinuity. Add a constant to make it positive. Choose summable positive coefficients giving a finite sum at the prescribed point (and at infinity if interior). Their sum is the required function. In dimension two, if the polar set contains infinity, add a positive multiple of $\log (|x-a|/R)$ on the exterior. In higher dimensions infinity cannot belong to a polar set. The same construction on a finite boundary singleton and epsilon comparison shows that its harmonic measure is zero. A local finite-point weak barrier can be upgraded on the bounded set $D=\Omega \cap B(a,r)$ by the proved bounded-domain weak-barrier theorem. Its strong barrier $g$ has a positive lower bound away from $a$. On a cutting sphere inside $B(a,r)$ choose $c>0$ below that lower bound; paste $\min (g,c)$ inside to the constant $c$ outside. They agree on a collar, so the pasted function is superharmonic, vanishes at $a$, and is bounded away from zero off every neighborhood of $a$. If infinity is interior, its value $c$ dominates every exterior sphere mean, since it is globally at most $c$. Thus the pasting remains valid there. The usual upper/lower barrier comparison proves regularity. Conversely use a bounded continuous boundary function $m\ge 0$ vanishing only at $a$. Its harmonic solution is positive on every component: otherwise its probability harmonic measure would be concentrated on the zero-mass singleton. At a regular point it tends to zero, giving a weak barrier. This avoids unbounded distance data on a boundary containing infinity. For a boundary infinity in $d\ge 3$, the fundamental function with any fixed finite pole is an explicit local weak barrier, positive and bounded away from zero on every bounded portion away from infinity. In dimension two inversion has multiplier one and transfers the finite-point local barrier criterion. At all finite points inversion preserves weak barriers locally. Thus the bounded-domain Kellogg theorem transfers to the inverted domain; polar sets transfer by Kelvin transformation. In $d\ge 3$ the possible extra center corresponds to an already regular infinity. This proves polar irregularity in all cases under the present nondensity hypothesis. $\square$

title: Lemma 4.4.16
section: 4.4 Perron theory and fine boundary limits
text: Lemma 4.4.16 . 5D12CB9707B5 On every proper domain with nonpolar complement a polar boundary set has a positive superharmonic blow-up function, finite at a prescribed interior point. A bounded harmonic function with zero boundary limits outside a polar set is zero. Proof. Only the dense case remains. Work in a connected component, choose $a\in \Omega $, and concentric closed balls with $0<r_0<r_1<r_2<r_3$, all contained in $\Omega $. Removing the smallest ball gives a nondense domain. Its pole function $v$ can be harmonically lowered on the annulus $r_0<|x-a|<r_3$, so it is finite harmonic near the two middle spheres. This preserves its true-boundary blow-up and positivity. Write $O=\Omega \setminus \overline{B(a,r_1)}$. This set is connected: any path in $\Omega $ entering the removed ball can be rerouted through the contained annulus. The harmonic measure $Q$ of its inner sphere is strictly below one on $O$. Indeed the original nonpolar boundary contains a regular point, since the nondense Kellogg exception is polar; $Q$ tends to zero there. The strong maximum principle then gives $q=\max _{|x-a|=r_2}Q(x)<1$. Set $w_0=0$. Given $w_{j-1}$, let $u_ j$ be the ball solution in $B(a,r_2)$ with data $v+w_{j-1}$ on its sphere. Let $w_ j$ be the bounded solution on $O$ with data $u_ j-v$ on the inner sphere and zero on the true boundary. These are continuous boundary data on the nondense domain. For consecutive differences the ball maximum principle and the bound by $Q$ give \[  \| u_{j+1}-u_ j\| _{S_{r_1}} \le \| w_ j-w_{j-1}\| _{S_{r_2}},\qquad \| w_{j+1}-w_ j\| _{S_{r_2}} \le q\| u_{j+1}-u_ j\| _{S_{r_1}}.  \] Thus the corrections converge in geometric series, uniformly on the respective boundaries and hence throughout their domains. Their limits $u,w$ are harmonic; $w$ is bounded. On both annulus boundary spheres, $u=v+w$, so annular uniqueness gives this equality throughout the overlap. Paste $u$ inside to $v+w$ outside. The result is superharmonic, harmonic near $a$, bounded below, and has the same polar boundary blow-up as $v$. Adding a constant makes it positive. This proves the assertion including finiteness at the prescribed center. Componentwise construction proves the disconnected version. For bounded harmonic $h$ with zero boundary limits outside a polar $Z$, compare $\pm h+\varepsilon p$ with zero, where $p$ is the positive blow-up function, finite at a prescribed interior point. Compactified boundary comparison applies even on $Z$, and yields $|h(a)|\le \varepsilon p(a)$. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and choose $a$ arbitrarily. The same epsilon argument permits polar exceptions in bounded Perron competitors. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.4.17
section: 4.4 Perron theory and fine boundary limits
text: Theorem 4.4.17 . A7E357C38C8E On every proper compactified domain with nonpolar complement, continuous boundary data are resolutive, the irregular boundary points form a polar set, and bounded harmonic solutions are unique with polar boundary exceptions. The integral characterization of resolutive data holds: an extended function is resolutive exactly when it is integrable for the simultaneously completed harmonic measures, and then $H_ f(x)=\int f\, d\omega _ x$. Polar boundary sets have zero harmonic measure. Proof. For a dense domain remove an interior closed ball. Solve the continuous datum $f$ on the true boundary and the constant $M+1$ on the artificial sphere, where $|f|\le M$. Paste $M+1$ inside by taking the minimum with that constant on a collar. The resulting bounded superharmonic function is a global upper competitor. The lower construction uses $-M-1$. At every regular true boundary point of the punctured nondense domain, these give the corresponding boundary limits for the global upper/lower solutions. Their difference is bounded harmonic, with zero boundary limits outside the polar Kellogg set, and is zero by the preceding lemma. Thus $f$ is resolutive. Those same upper/lower bounds show each such punctured-domain regular point is regular for $\Omega $, proving Kellogg for the general domain. Local barriers and the capped-constant construction give the equivalent local criterion as before. The full measurable-data proof now uses precisely the steps established for bounded domains: closed boundary indicators by continuous decreasing approximation, the pi-lambda argument, nonnegative simple approximation, and monotone continuity of the upper envelope via summable positive errors at a fixed pole. The only local harmonic operations needed are lowering and monotone convergence, available for both interior and exterior balls. For clarity, the necessity step also survives unchanged: countably many upper/lower competitors approximating a finite solution at a pole give Borel boundary liminf/limsup sandwiches. Their integrals have the same value at that pole, so their difference is zero almost everywhere there; positive harmonicity and Harnack transfer this common null set throughout the component. The sandwiches identify the datum in the completed measure class and give its absolute integrability. Conversely positive and negative integrable parts follow from monotone simple functions, and null changes are removed by the sandwich comparison. Apply this separately in the countably many components. Epsilon comparison with the constructed pole functions proves polar boundary nullity. This establishes the same full equivalence as the bounded Perron theorem, now with the compactified boundary condition at infinity included explicitly. $\square$

Theorem 4.4.25 . 04CCB65ED650 Every endpoint of a nondegenerate planar segment is a nonthin point of that segment. If the complement of a planar open set is thin at $a$, arbitrarily small circles centered at $a$ lie in the open set. Consequently a boundary point belonging to a nondegenerate continuum in the complement is regular. In particular every bounded simply connected planar domain is regular. Proof. An interior point of a segment is regular for a disk slit along the segment by the explicit exterior-segment barrier. The boundary nonthinness theorem therefore makes the segment nonthin at that point. If it were thin at an endpoint, reflect an amplified barrier across the endpoint and add the two barriers. The doubled segment would then be thin at its interior point, a contradiction. The radial projection $y\mapsto a+|y-a|e_1$ is a contraction preserving distances from $a$. If every sufficiently small circle met a thin complement, its projection would contain a nondegenerate segment ending at $a$, contradicting contraction invariance of thinness. Hence the required circles exist. An exterior continuum containing $a$ and another point $b$ meets every circle of radius less than $|a-b|$, by connectedness of its distance image. The last assertion follows without Cauchy–Schwarz: $I(\lambda )\le I(\mu ,\lambda )=\int G\lambda \, d\mu \le I(\mu )$. To prove no polar mass, take a positive pole function $w$ on a Borel polar carrier $P$. On compact subsets $K$ of $P\cap \{ G\mu \le j\} $ the restricted measure has bounded potential on its support, so the everywhere-finite domination theorem, applied to $\varepsilon w$, gives $G(\mu |_ K)=0$. Thus $\mu (K)=0$. Inner regularity and $\mu (\{ G\mu =\infty \} )=0$ give $\mu (P)=0$. Every polar subset has a Borel polar carrier. Conversely a nonpolar Borel set has a compact subset of positive capacity, whose nonzero equilibrium measure has finite energy and gives it positive mass. We establish Cauchy–Schwarz without assuming positivity for signed energies. For compact $K$ and continuous $f$ on $K$, the functional $J_ f(\eta )=I(\eta )-2\int f\, d\eta $ has a minimizer among positive measures on $K$ (the empty case is immediate). Positivity and compactness give a finite $ eta >0$ with $G\ge  eta $ on $K	imes K$, hence $J_ f(\eta )\ge  eta \eta (K)^2-2\| f\| _\infty \eta (K)$, bounding the masses of a minimizing sequence. Compact measure selection and the continuous kernels $\min (G,m)$ give lower semicontinuity of energy: weak convergence of the product measures follows first for products of continuous functions, then for all continuous functions by their uniformly dense algebra. The zero measure gives a finite infimum, so the minimizer $\eta $ has finite energy. Variations $\eta -t\eta |_ U$, for $0<t<1$, give $G\eta \le f$ on its support. Variations adding the equilibrium measure of $K\cap \{ f-G\eta \ge \varepsilon \} $ give $G\eta \ge f$ quasi-everywhere on $K$. In these expansions all mutual integrals are finite: the adding measure has bounded potential, and the removing measure is a restriction of $\eta $. For compactly supported $\mu ,
u \in \mathcal E^+$ choose continuous $0\le f\le G\mu $ on their common compact support and let $\eta $ be this minimizer. The no-polar-mass assertion gives $I(\eta )=\int f\, d\eta $. The inequality $J_ f(t

u \le \|

Thus domination applies and gives $G\eta \le G\mu $ and hence $\| \eta \| \le \| \mu \| $. Increase continuous minorants to $G\mu $ to obtain Cauchy–Schwarz. Compact restrictions and monotone convergence prove it for arbitrary finite-energy measures. title: Theorem 4.5.4
text:
Theorem 4.5.4 . CE0D5F4DF7B2 The cone $\mathcal E^+$ is complete in the energy norm. On energy-bounded sequences in this cone, vague convergence is equivalent to weak energy convergence. A strong Cauchy sequence converges strongly whenever it converges weakly. If finite-energy potentials converge monotonically to a finite-energy potential, their measures converge strongly. Signed compactly supported finite-energy measures with continuous compactly supported Green potentials are dense in $\mathcal E$. Proof. In any inner product space weak lower semicontinuity of the norm follows from $\| z\| ^2=\lim \langle z_ j,zangle \le \| z\| \liminf \| z_ j\| $. Apply this to $z_ j=\mu _ j-\mu _ k$ to prove the strong-Cauchy/weak-limit assertion. If $p_ j=G\mu _ j\le G\mu _ k=p_ k$, then reciprocity gives \[  \| \mu _ k-\mu _ j\| ^2 \le \| \mu _ k\| ^2-\| \mu _ j\| ^2.  \] Thus monotone potentials give a strong Cauchy sequence: in the increasing case the norms are bounded by the limit norm, and in the decreasing case by the first norm, with the inequality direction reversed for the lower bound. Dominated or monotone integration of $p_ j$ against every finite-energy measure proves weak convergence to the prescribed limit. For density, compact restrictions of $\mu $ converge strongly: their tail energies tend to zero by dominated convergence for the integrable kernel $G\, d\mu \, d\mu $. On each compact support, Lusin's theorem and the support-continuity argument split a measure of finite energy into disjoint compact restrictions with finite continuous potentials; finiteness is needed only almost everywhere for the original measure. Finite partial sums again converge strongly. For one such compact continuous potential $p$, let $D_ j$ be a regular exhaustion containing its support and put $q_ j=p$ outside $D_ j$, $q_ j=H^{D_ j}_ p$ inside. Sweeping makes $q_ j=G
u _ j$ a potential, with compactly supported $
u _ j$, and $q_ j\downarrow 0$. The preceding monotone assertion gives $
u _ j	o 0$ strongly. Then $\mu -
u _ j$ has compact support, and its Green potential $p-q_ j$ is continuous and compactly supported. Differences prove signed density. Energy-bounded positive measures have uniformly bounded masses on each compact $K$: choose nonnegative $q\in C_ c^\infty $ equal to one on $K$, and use its signed finite-energy representing measure $\lambda $ above: $\mu _ j(K)\le \int q\, d\mu _ j\le \| \lambda \| \| \mu _ j\| $. Weak energy convergence therefore implies convergence on smooth compact tests and then on every continuous compact test by uniform approximation in a fixed compact neighborhood. Conversely a vague limit $\mu $ has $I(\mu )\le \liminf I(\mu _ j)$: insert compact cutoffs in both kernel variables, truncate the kernel, pass to product weak convergence, and increase cutoffs and truncations. Thus $\mu \in \mathcal E^+$. Vague convergence gives convergence against the dense compact-potential tests; Cauchy–Schwarz and the uniform energy bound extend it to every energy test, proving weak convergence. Finally a strong Cauchy sequence in the positive cone has bounded energy and locally bounded masses. Diagonal compact measure selection gives a vaguely convergent subsequence and positive Radon limit. The preceding paragraph makes it an energy weak limit, and the strong-Cauchy assertion makes the whole sequence converge strongly. No completeness of the signed space was assumed. $\square$

title: Example 4.5.5
text: Example 4.5.5 . 61A5D2A82793 A finite-energy potential may be infinite on a nonempty compact polar set $Z$. Choose open neighborhoods $U_ j\Supset Z$ with $C(U_ j)<2^{-4j}$ and common compact closure. Their equilibrium measures $\mu _ j$ have $G\mu _ j=1$ on $Z$ and $\| \mu _ j\| \le 2^{-2j}$. Cauchy–Schwarz and monotone convergence give finite energy for $\sum \mu _ j$, whose potential is infinite on $Z$. The signed energy space is nevertheless incomplete. In $\mathbb R^3$ let $\sigma _ r$ be uniform mass one on the sphere of radius $r$, and put $\lambda _ j=\sigma _{1-4^{-j}}-\sigma _1$. The spherical potential formula gives $\| \lambda _ j\| ^2=(4^ j-1)^{-1}$, so the partial sums are energy Cauchy. If they had a signed Radon energy limit $\lambda $, testing against $q=G(-\Delta q/c_3)$ for $q\in C_ c^\infty $ supported in the open unit ball would show $\lambda |_{B(0,1)}=\sum _ j\sigma _{1-4^{-j}}$. Indeed only finitely many spheres meet each such support, and energy convergence passes these tests. This positive restriction has infinite mass in the closed unit ball, contradicting local finiteness of the positive variation of $\lambda $. This argument avoids passing an unbounded-mass sequence through arbitrary uniformly approximating test functions.

The affine functional differs from $\| \mu -

title: 4.5.7 The Martin boundary
text:
Throughout this section $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ is connected and Greenian, and $a\in \Omega $ is fixed. We use compact Hausdorff compactifications, finite Radon measures on compact spaces, Tychonoff's theorem, the compact-metric Riesz representation theorem, Tietze extension, and the lattice Stone–Weierstrass theorem as explicit general topology and functional analysis prerequisites. None of these is an assumed Martin representation theorem. Lemma 4.5.8 . D878F27BAB16 For any family $\mathcal Q$ of extended continuous functions on $\Omega $, there is a unique compactification in which these functions extend and separate boundary points. It is the closure of the evaluation map into $[-\infty ,\infty ]^{\mathcal Q\cup C_ c(\Omega )}$. Proof. Compact-support functions separate interior points and recover their original neighborhoods by positive bumps, so the evaluation map is an embedding. Each bump's nonzero set in the closure lies in the image of its compact support; thus the interior image is open and its complement is the boundary. All compact-support coordinates vanish on the boundary, so the remaining coordinates separate its points. For any other such compactification the coordinate extensions define a continuous injection into the same product, with exactly this closure as image by density. A continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism, proving uniqueness fixing $\Omega $. $\square$ Choose $\alpha $ so large that $\{ G(\cdot ,a)\ge \alpha \} \Subset \Omega $; the Green bound away from its pole permits this choice. Take a smooth increasing concave function $\phi $ equal to $t$ for $t\le \alpha $ and constant for $t\ge \alpha +1$. Set $b=\phi (G(\cdot ,a))$. It is positive, smooth, superharmonic, constant near $a$, and a potential: it is bounded by the potential $G(\cdot ,a)$. Its Riesz measure has compact support. Put $k_ y(x)=G(y,x)/b(y)$. The compactification associated with the functions $y\mapsto k_ y(x)$ is denoted $M$, with boundary $\Delta $. Theorem 4.5.9 . 9D6B5CF5E0CF The extended kernel $K(y,x)$ on $M	imes \Omega $ is positive and jointly continuous, with extended values only on the interior diagonal. For $y\in \Delta $, $K_ y$ is harmonic and $K_ y(a)=1$. Distinct points of $M$ give nonproportional kernels. The space $M$ is compact metrizable: for a countable dense set $\{ x_ j\} $ in $\Omega $ the metric is \[  ho (y,z)=\sum _{j\ge 1}2^{-j} \left| rac{K(y,x_ j)}{1+K(y,x_ j)}-  rac{K(z,x_ j)}{1+K(z,x_ j)}ight|.  \] Proof. For $C\Subset W\Subset \Omega $ containing $a$, Harnack comparison in the pole variable, or sweeping onto a compact neighborhood of $C$, bounds $G(y,x)/G(y,a)$ uniformly for $x\in C$, $y
otin W$. For the sweeping proof, both pole functions equal their compact reductions off that neighborhood: they are bounded harmonic there and have the same boundary values outside a polar exception, so compactified uniqueness applies. Their boundary values on its compact interior boundary have uniform positive lower and finite upper bounds, giving the ratio bound. A general compact $C$ is enlarged to include $a$. Since $b=G(\cdot ,a)$ off a compact set, these bounds also hold for $k$. Normal convergence and the derivative estimates for bounded harmonic families show that every boundary kernel is harmonic, and that convergence in the compactification is locally uniform in $x$. This proves joint continuity at boundary points. Interior joint continuity is that of $G$, and $K_ y(a)=1$ on the boundary follows from the same identity off the cutoff compact. Positivity follows from the harmonic minimum principle. Interior kernels are distinguished by their poles. A boundary kernel has no interior pole. For two boundary points, proportionality and the value one at $a$ imply equality of every defining coordinate, hence equality of the points. More explicitly, $b=G\lambda _0$ with compactly supported $\lambda _0$; therefore $\int K(y,x)d\lambda _0(x)=1$, first for interior $y$, then on the boundary by joint continuity near that compact support. This supplies the normalization and the ratio representation of defining coordinates used in Helms 12.4 as well. The countable coordinates in the displayed formula separate points: density and extended continuity in $x$ recover every kernel. They define a continuous injection of compact $M$ into a countable cube, hence a homeomorphism onto its image. The uniformly convergent sum metric on that cube induces the given topology. No sequential compactness is assumed before this argument. $\square$ For a measure $\mu $ on $M$ write $K\mu (x)=\int K(y,x)d\mu (y)$ when not identically infinite. It is superharmonic. Its interior part is the Green potential of $b^{-1}\mu |_\Omega $, and its boundary part is harmonic by the compact kernel bounds. In particular equality of two $K$-potentials determines their interior measures, by the distributional Riesz identity. For $q\in C_ c^2(\Omega )$ put $\lambda =(-\Delta (qb)/c_ d)dx$. Then \[  q(y)=\int K(y,x)d\lambda (x),\qquad y\in \Omega .  \] This is the distributional Green identity for the compact test $qb$. The measure $\lambda $ has bounded density and compact support, so every defined $K$-potential is $|\lambda |$-integrable by local integrability. This also proves the test-function assertion 12.6 and the interior uniqueness assertion 12.7 without an undefined signed potential. Lemma 4.5.10 . B0A113187C30 For relatively closed $F\subset \Omega $ and $u\ge 0$ superharmonic, $\widehat R_ Fu=K\mu $ for a measure supported on its closure in $M$. Every positive harmonic function has such a representation supported on $\Delta $. For compact $C\Subset \Omega $, write $\mu _ C$ for the unique interior measure representing $\widehat R_ C(K\mu )$. For boundary $y$ write $\gamma _{y,C}=(\delta _ y)_ C$. The operator \[  T_ Cf(y)=\int f\, d\gamma _{y,C},\qquad y\in \Delta ,  \] maps $C(M)$ positively and continuously into $C(\Delta )$. If $C$ contains the cutoff compact in its interior, $T_ C1=1$ and $\| T_ C\| =1$. Proof. Exhaust $F$ by compact $F_ j$. The compact reductions are potentials $G
u _ j=K(b
u _ j)$, with supports in $F_ j$. At a point $x$ where $u(x)$ is finite the strictly positive minimum of $K(\cdot ,x)$ on $M$ bounds their masses. Choose a weak limit $\mu $. For a sphere compactly inside $\Omega $, its average of $K(y,\cdot )$ is a finite continuous function of $y\in M$: away from the sphere use joint bounded continuity; on it use the proved continuity of spherical Green averages after cancellation of the integrable fundamental singularity. Thus weak convergence and monotone convergence of reductions identify all spherical averages of $K\mu $ and $\widehat R_ Fu$. Fatou first bounds $K\mu \le u$, so it is defined. Let the sphere radius tend to zero to get equality everywhere. For harmonic $u=h$, take $F=\Omega $ and compact neighborhoods $F_ j$ exhausting it. The reduction equals $h$ on their interiors and its measure is supported on their boundaries; these escape every interior compact, so the limit measure lies on $\Delta $. The representing compact measure is unique by the interior Riesz identity. To prove continuity of $T_ C$, uniform continuity of $K$ on $\Delta 	imes C$ shows that $K_ y$ and $K_ z$ differ there by at most $\varepsilon $ when $y,z$ are close. Fix a positive harmonic kernel bounded below on $C$; its multiple $v$ majorizes one there. Order and subadditivity of reductions give $|K\gamma _{y,C}-K\gamma _{z,C}|\le \varepsilon \widehat R_ Cv$. Testing the signed bounded-density representation of $q\in C_ c^2$ above therefore bounds $|T_ Cq(y)-T_ Cq(z)|$ by a constant times $\varepsilon $. The masses are uniformly bounded since $\int K(t,a)d\gamma _{y,C}(t)=\widehat R_ CK_ y(a)\le 1$ and $\inf _{t\in C}K(t,a)>0$. Approximate restrictions of arbitrary $f\in C(M)$ uniformly on $C$ by smooth compactly supported functions; this proves continuity of $T_ Cf$. When the cutoff compact lies in $\operatorname {int}C$, the measure is on $\partial C$, where $K(t,a)=1$, and the reduction at $a$ equals $K_ y(a)=1$. Hence its mass is one, proving the last assertion. $\square$ Lemma 4.5.11 . FDE7BF6A9927 Regularized reduction onto relatively closed $F$ commutes with nonnegative integrals of a jointly Borel family $u_ t$ of superharmonic functions, provided $\int u_ t(x_0)d\eta (t)<\infty $ somewhere. If every reduced function is a potential, their integral is a potential. In particular $\mu _ C=\int \gamma _{y,C}d\mu (y)$ for measures on $\Delta $. Proof. Off a common polar set of irregular boundary points, closed sweeping is the identity on $F$ and the harmonic-measure integral off $F$, with zero on the original boundary. These kernels are Borel: for continuous compact tests their integrals are continuous in the pole; a countable monotone class gives indicators and all nonnegative Borel tests. Since the Euclidean second factor is second countable, its product Borel sigma algebra is generated by rectangles. Thus the reduced family is jointly Borel off that common polar set. Extend it by zero there and recover its actual canonical values by limits of ball averages; these averages are jointly Borel, so the recovered family is jointly Borel everywhere. The integral is lsc by Fatou and super-mean-valued by Tonelli, and is finite at $x_0$ because reduction is at most $u_ t$. Outside the common polar set, Tonelli in the harmonic-measure formula identifies it with the reduction of the integral. Canonical ball averages give equality everywhere. Only a sigma-finite effective parameter set is needed: the sets $\{ u_ t(x_0)>1/m\} $ have finite measure, and a nonnegative superharmonic function zero at $x_0$ vanishes identically. For potentials, lower harmonically along a regular exhaustion. Each minorant decreases to zero; its integral is dominated at $x_0$ by the integrable $u_ t(x_0)$. Dominated convergence gives zero greatest harmonic minorant of the integral. Interior uniqueness proves the measure identity. $\square$ Theorem 4.5.12 . 6736FBE7368C Let $\Delta _1$ be the boundary points for which $K_ y$ generates an extreme ray of the cone of positive harmonic functions. This is a $G_\delta $ subset of $M$. Every positive harmonic $h$ has a unique finite measure $
u $ carried by $\Delta _1$ such that $h=K
u $; its mass is $h(a)$. Proof. We supply the uniqueness mechanism rather than assuming a simplex theorem. If a nonzero $K\mu $ generates an extreme ray of positive superharmonic functions, every restriction of $\mu $ to a neighborhood of a support point has potential proportional to $K\mu $. Normalize these restrictions to represent $K\mu $. At a finite interior test point away from the support point, positivity bounds their masses. Shrinking the neighborhoods makes their kernels converge uniformly at each other test point, so their limit is $c\delta _ y$ and $K\mu =cK_ y$. Nonproportionality of distinct kernels forces the support to be that single point. For harmonic $K\mu $ its support is on $\Delta $, so the point is in $\Delta _1$. Choose nested compact neighborhoods $C_ j$ exhausting $\Omega $ and containing the cutoff compact in their interiors. Put $T_ j=T_{C_ j}$. For $y\in \Delta _1$, every weak cluster of the probability measures $\gamma _{y,C_ j}$ represents $K_ y$: their supports escape interior compacts, where the kernel singularities lie, and their potentials equal $K_ y$ eventually at each interior test point. Extremality and the preceding support assertion force this cluster to be $\delta _ y$. Thus $\gamma _{y,C_ j}	o \delta _ y$. Conversely, if this convergence holds along an exhaustion and $K_ y=K\mu +K\eta $, additivity and interior uniqueness give $\gamma _{y,C_ j}=\mu _{C_ j}+\eta _{C_ j}$. Weak clusters of these positive measures sum to $\delta _ y$ and represent the respective harmonic functions. Each is proportional to $\delta _ y$, proving extremality. This convergence criterion also makes $\Delta _1$ Borel: require convergence of $T_ jf_ l(y)$ to $f_ l(y)$ for a countable dense family, expressed by countable intersections and unions of the open error sets. These arguments also show that for any measure $
u $ carried by $\Delta _1$, $
u _{C_ j}	o 
u $ by dominated integration of $T_ jf	o f$. Consequently two such measures representing the same function agree. For existence start with any boundary representing measure $\mu $ and take a subsequence $\mu _{C_ j}	o 
u $, still supported on $\Delta $ in the limit and representing $K\mu $. For this subsequence let $\mathcal L$ be the continuous functions $f$ on $M$ for which $T_ jf	o f$ in $
u $-measure. It is a linear space containing constants. It is a lattice: if $g_1,g_2\in \mathcal L$, positivity gives $T_ j(g_1\wedge g_2)\le T_ jg_1\wedge T_ jg_2$. The right side tends in measure and integral to $g_1\wedge g_2$. The integral of the left side is $\int (g_1\wedge g_2)d
u _{C_ j}= \int (g_1\wedge g_2)d\mu _{C_ j}$, tending to the same value by the chosen weak convergence. Their nonnegative difference therefore tends to zero in $L^1$, proving the lattice assertion. The space contains $C_ c(\Omega )$, whose restrictions and $T_ j$ values on $\Delta $ are eventually zero. It also contains every continuous function agreeing with $K(\cdot ,x)$ outside an interior compact: for large $j$, $T_ jf=K(\cdot ,x)=f$ on $\Delta $. These functions separate boundary points, while compact bumps separate the other points. Lattice Stone–Weierstrass makes $\mathcal L$ dense in $C(M)$. The unit contraction bound for $T_ j$ makes it uniformly closed, hence all of $C(M)$. For a countable dense family choose a common subsequence converging $
u $-almost everywhere. At almost every $y$, $\gamma _{y,C_ j}	o \delta _ y$ along this subsequence, which is still an exhaustion; the converse criterion makes $y\in \Delta _1$. This proves existence and the mass identity follows by evaluation at $a$. For the topology choose a countable dense family $f_ l$ in $C(M)$. The criterion just proved identifies $\Delta _1$ with \[   igcap _{m,k\ge 1}\   igcup _{j\ge k}  igcap _{l\le m}\{ y\in \Delta :|T_ jf_ l(y)-f_ l(y)|<1/m\} .  \] This formula requires simultaneous approximation of finitely many tests. Each inner finite intersection is relatively open; a diagonal subsequence proves its converse. Since $\Delta $ is closed in compact metric $M$, it is itself $G_\delta $, proving the assertion in $M$. $\square$ Theorem 4.5.13 . 0E65F552B1A6 Let $\chi $ be the minimal representing measure of the constant one. Every $f\in C(\Delta )$ is resolutive for the Perron classes defined by limits in $M$, and its solution is $H_ f(x)=\int K(y,x)f(y)d\chi (y)$. For a ball with reference point its center, $M$ is the closed ball, $\Delta _1=\Delta $ is its sphere, and the normalized boundary kernel is $R^{d-2}(R^2-|x|^2)/|y-x|^ d$. Proof. Compactness of $M$ and the interior strong minimum principle prove the boundary minimum principle, so the upper/lower Perron constructions and harmonic alternatives apply. If $y\in \Delta _1$ and $U$ is a neighborhood of $y$ in $M$, then $p=\widehat R_{\Omega \setminus U}K_ y$ is a potential. Indeed its greatest harmonic minorant, being below the minimal $K_ y$, is $tK_ y$, $0\le t\le 1$. The case $t=1$ would represent the extreme $K_ y$ on $M\setminus U$, impossible by the support assertion. Write $p=w+tK_ y$ with $w$ a potential. Idempotence and additivity of reduction give $w+tK_ y=\widehat R_{\Omega \setminus U}w+tw+t^2K_ y$. Uniqueness of Riesz decomposition yields $t=t^2$, hence $t=0$. Extend $f$ continuously to $M$ and first assume $0\le f\le 1$. Partition $\Delta _1$ into the bins $E_ i=\{ (i-1/2)/j\le f<(i+1/2)/j\} $, $0\le i\le j$, and put $h_ i=K(\chi |_{E_ i})$, so $\sum h_ i=1$. Let $F_ i=\{ x\in \Omega :|f(x)-i/j|\ge 1/j\} $. The preceding local-potential assertion and the integral-sweeping lemma make $p_ i=\widehat R_{F_ i}h_ i$ a potential. On $F_ i$, $p_ i=h_ i$ quasi-everywhere; off $F_ i$, $(i-1)/j<f<(i+1)/j$. Therefore \[  \sum _{i=1}^ j rac{i-1}{j}(h_ i-p_ i)\le f \le \sum _{i=0}^ j rac{i+1}{j}h_ i+\sum _{i=0}^ jp_ i.  \] Initially the inequalities hold quasi-everywhere; canonical ball averages and continuity of $f$ give them everywhere. The left and right sides are bounded lower and upper competitors respectively. Taking harmonic minorants removes their potential terms: every harmonic minorant of a potential is at most zero. Thus the lower/upper solutions are between $\sum _{i\ge 1}(i-1)h_ i/j$ and $\sum _{i\ge 0}(i+1)h_ i/j$, a gap at most $2/j$. The same bounds enclose $K(f\chi )$. Letting $j	o \infty $ proves the formula, and scaling and adding constants handle arbitrary continuous data. For the ball, expand $G(r	heta ,x)$ in $R-r$, uniformly for $	heta $ near a specified boundary point. The reference normal derivative is nonzero and bounded away from zero there; the quotient therefore tends along every approach to the quotient of normal derivatives. The explicit ball kernel gives precisely the normalized Poisson kernel displayed above. It separates sphere points, so uniqueness of function compactification identifies $M$ with the closed ball. We also verify the uniqueness needed in this example. For continuous sphere data $g$, the symmetry $P_ B(t\zeta ,y)=P_ B(ty,\zeta )$ and the ball approximate-identity estimate give \[  \int _{\partial B}g(\zeta )P_ B(t\zeta ,y)d\sigma (\zeta )\longrightarrow g(y)  \] uniformly in $y$ as $t\uparrow 1$. Uniformity follows from uniform continuity of $g$, kernel mass one and a uniformly vanishing distant tail. Finite signed Fubini therefore recovers every continuous integral of a boundary measure from its interior Poisson function; equal functions have equal boundary measures. Now if $0\le h\le K_ y$, represent both $h$ and $K_ y-h$ by positive ball boundary measures. Their sum is the point mass representing $K_ y$, by this uniqueness, so each is supported on $\{ y\} $. Thus the sphere kernels are minimal and $\Delta _1=\Delta $. This argument supplies uniform control even for tangential approaches. $\square$

title: Lemma 4.5.8
text: Lemma 4.5.8 . D878F27BAB16 For any family $\mathcal Q$ of extended continuous functions on $\Omega $, there is a unique compactification in which these functions extend and separate boundary points. It is the closure of the evaluation map into $[-\infty ,\infty ]^{\mathcal Q\cup C_ c(\Omega )}$. Proof. Compact-support functions separate interior points and recover their original neighborhoods by positive bumps, so the evaluation map is an embedding. Each bump's nonzero set in the closure lies in the image of its compact support; thus the interior image is open and its complement is the boundary. All compact-support coordinates vanish on the boundary, so the remaining coordinates separate its points. For any other such compactification the coordinate extensions define a continuous injection into the same product, with exactly this closure as image by density. A continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism, proving uniqueness fixing $\Omega $. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.5.9
text: Theorem 4.5.9 . 9D6B5CF5E0CF The extended kernel $K(y,x)$ on $M\times \Omega $ is positive and jointly continuous, with extended values only on the interior diagonal. For $y\in \Delta $, $K_ y$ is harmonic and $K_ y(a)=1$. Distinct points of $M$ give nonproportional kernels. The space $M$ is compact metrizable: for a countable dense set $\{ x_ j\} $ in $\Omega $ the metric is \[  \rho (y,z)=\sum _{j\ge 1}2^{-j} \left|\frac{K(y,x_ j)}{1+K(y,x_ j)}- \frac{K(z,x_ j)}{1+K(z,x_ j)}\right|.  \] Proof. For $C\Subset W\Subset \Omega $ containing $a$, Harnack comparison in the pole variable, or sweeping onto a compact neighborhood of $C$, bounds $G(y,x)/G(y,a)$ uniformly for $x\in C$, $y\notin W$. For the sweeping proof, both pole functions equal their compact reductions off that neighborhood: they are bounded harmonic there and have the same boundary values outside a polar exception, so compactified uniqueness applies. Their boundary values on its compact interior boundary have uniform positive lower and finite upper bounds, giving the ratio bound. A general compact $C$ is enlarged to include $a$. Since $b=G(\cdot ,a)$ off a compact set, these bounds also hold for $k$. Normal convergence and the derivative estimates for bounded harmonic families show that every boundary kernel is harmonic, and that convergence in the compactification is locally uniform in $x$. This proves joint continuity at boundary points. Interior joint continuity is that of $G$, and $K_ y(a)=1$ on the boundary follows from the same identity off the cutoff compact. Positivity follows from the harmonic minimum principle. Interior kernels are distinguished by their poles. A boundary kernel has no interior pole. For two boundary points, proportionality and the value one at $a$ imply equality of every defining coordinate, hence equality of the points. More explicitly, $b=G\lambda _0$ with compactly supported $\lambda _0$; therefore $\int K(y,x)d\lambda _0(x)=1$, first for interior $y$, then on the boundary by joint continuity near that compact support. This supplies the normalization and the ratio representation of defining coordinates used in Helms 12.4 as well. The countable coordinates in the displayed formula separate points: density and extended continuity in $x$ recover every kernel. They define a continuous injection of compact $M$ into a countable cube, hence a homeomorphism onto its image. The uniformly convergent sum metric on that cube induces the given topology. No sequential compactness is assumed before this argument. $\square$

title: Lemma 4.5.10
text: Lemma 4.5.10 . B0A113187C30 For relatively closed $F\subset \Omega $ and $u\ge 0$ superharmonic, $\widehat R_ Fu=K\mu $ for a measure supported on its closure in $M$. Every positive harmonic function has such a representation supported on $\Delta $. For compact $C\Subset \Omega $, write $\mu _ C$ for the unique interior measure representing $\widehat R_ C(K\mu )$. For boundary $y$ write $\gamma _{y,C}=(\delta _ y)_ C$. The operator \[  T_ Cf(y)=\int f\, d\gamma _{y,C},\qquad y\in \Delta ,  \] maps $C(M)$ positively and continuously into $C(\Delta )$. If $C$ contains the cutoff compact in its interior, $T_ C1=1$ and $\| T_ C\| =1$. Proof. Exhaust $F$ by compact $F_ j$. The compact reductions are potentials $G\nu _ j=K(b\nu _ j)$, with supports in $F_ j$. At a point $x$ where $u(x)$ is finite the strictly positive minimum of $K(\cdot ,x)$ on $M$ bounds their masses. Choose a weak limit $\mu $. For a sphere compactly inside $\Omega $, its average of $K(y,\cdot )$ is a finite continuous function of $y\in M$: away from the sphere use joint bounded continuity; on it use the proved continuity of spherical Green averages after cancellation of the integrable fundamental singularity. Thus weak convergence and monotone convergence of reductions identify all spherical averages of $K\mu $ and $\widehat R_ Fu$. Fatou first bounds $K\mu \le u$, so it is defined. Let the sphere radius tend to zero to get equality everywhere. For harmonic $u=h$, take $F=\Omega $ and compact neighborhoods $F_ j$ exhausting it. The reduction equals $h$ on their interiors and its measure is supported on their boundaries; these escape every interior compact, so the limit measure lies on $\Delta $. The representing compact measure is unique by the interior Riesz identity. To prove continuity of $T_ C$, uniform continuity of $K$ on $\Delta \times C$ shows that $K_ y$ and $K_ z$ differ there by at most $\varepsilon $ when $y,z$ are close. Fix a positive harmonic kernel bounded below on $C$; its multiple $v$ majorizes one there. Order and subadditivity of reductions give $|K\gamma _{y,C}-K\gamma _{z,C}|\le \varepsilon \widehat R_ Cv$. Testing the signed bounded-density representation of $q\in C_ c^2$ above therefore bounds $|T_ Cq(y)-T_ Cq(z)|$ by a constant times $\varepsilon $. The masses are uniformly bounded since $\int K(t,a)d\gamma _{y,C}(t)=\widehat R_ CK_ y(a)\le 1$ and $\inf _{t\in C}K(t,a)>0$. Approximate restrictions of arbitrary $f\in C(M)$ uniformly on $C$ by smooth compactly supported functions; this proves continuity of $T_ Cf$. When the cutoff compact lies in $\operatorname {int}C$, the measure is on $\partial C$, where $K(t,a)=1$, and the reduction at $a$ equals $K_ y(a)=1$. Hence its mass is one, proving the last assertion. $\square$

title: Lemma 4.5.11
text: Lemma 4.5.11 . FDE7BF6A9927 Regularized reduction onto relatively closed $F$ commutes with nonnegative integrals of a jointly Borel family $u_ t$ of superharmonic functions, provided $\int u_ t(x_0)d\eta (t)<\infty $ somewhere. If every reduced function is a potential, their integral is a potential. In particular $\mu _ C=\int \gamma _{y,C}d\mu (y)$ for measures on $\Delta $. Proof. Off a common polar set of irregular boundary points, closed sweeping is the identity on $F$ and the harmonic-measure integral off $F$, with zero on the original boundary. These kernels are Borel: for continuous compact tests their integrals are continuous in the pole; a countable monotone class gives indicators and all nonnegative Borel tests. Since the Euclidean second factor is second countable, its product Borel sigma algebra is generated by rectangles. Thus the reduced family is jointly Borel off that common polar set. Extend it by zero there and recover its actual canonical values by limits of ball averages; these averages are jointly Borel, so the recovered family is jointly Borel everywhere. The integral is lsc by Fatou and super-mean-valued by Tonelli, and is finite at $x_0$ because reduction is at most $u_ t$. Outside the common polar set, Tonelli in the harmonic-measure formula identifies it with the reduction of the integral. Canonical ball averages give equality everywhere. Only a sigma-finite effective parameter set is needed: the sets $\{ u_ t(x_0)>1/m\} $ have finite measure, and a nonnegative superharmonic function zero at $x_0$ vanishes identically. For potentials, lower harmonically along a regular exhaustion. Each minorant decreases to zero; its integral is dominated at $x_0$ by the integrable $u_ t(x_0)$. Dominated convergence gives zero greatest harmonic minorant of the integral. Interior uniqueness proves the measure identity. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.5.12
text:
Theorem 4.5.12 . 6736FBE7368C Let $\Delta _1$ be the boundary points for which $K_ y$ generates an extreme ray of the cone of positive harmonic functions. This is a $G_\delta $ subset of $M$. Every positive harmonic $h$ has a unique finite measure $

Normalize these restrictions to represent $K\mu $. At a finite interior test point away from the support point, positivity bounds their masses. Shrinking the neighborhoods makes their kernels converge uniformly at each other test point, so their limit is $c\delta _ y$ and $K\mu =cK_ y$.
